*docs-advanced_features-hicache_storage_runtime_attach_detach-3-3-detach-disable-the-storage-backend*
3.3 Detach (disable) the storage backend

[Command]

[Command]Command

>sh
    curl -s -X DELETE http://127.0.0.1:30000/hicache/storage-backend \
      -H "Authorization: Bearer ${SGLANG_ADMIN_API_KEY}"
<
Notes:

- Detach only makes SGLang stop using the L3 storage backend and stops
  prefetch/backup threads
- It does not automatically delete data stored in Mooncake/HF3FS (or other
  remote backends)

 * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * *

*docs-advanced_features-hicache_storage_runtime_attach_detach-4-behavior-and-caveats*
4. BEHAVIOR AND CAVEATS

- No restart required: attach/detach switches in-process at runtime
- Must be idle: otherwise the request is rejected to avoid consistency
  issues
- Host KV layout constraints still apply: for example, Mooncake still
  requires layouts like `page_first/page_first_direct/page_head`; if the
  server's HiCache host-memory layout does not satisfy the backend
  requirements, attach will fail with an error
- Observability:
  - After attach, `server_args.hicache_storage_backend*` is updated on both
    the tokenizer and scheduler sides
  - If metrics are enabled, attach will create a storage metrics collector
    in `UnifiedRadixCache` on demand

----------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                *sglang-docs-advanced_features-hisparse_guide*
HiSparse: Hierarchical Sparse Attention

HiSparse reduces per-request GPU memory consumption during the decode phase
by maintaining only a small “hot” KV buffer on GPU while keeping complete KV
data in CPU pinned memory. Combined with PD disaggregation, it enables
significantly higher decode concurrency.

  Prerequisites: HiSparse works with models that use DeepSeek Sparse
  Attention (DSA) architectures (e.g., DeepSeek-V3.2, GLM-5.1, and the DSA
  layers of Kimi-K3.1), DeepSeek V4, and MiniMax M3. These models natively
  select a subset of tokens for attention, making it possible to keep only
  the top-k KV on GPU while storing the full KV in host memory --- without
  accuracy loss. Additionally, HiSparse currently requires PD disaggregation
  mode and is enabled on the decode instance only.

WHY HISPARSE?             *docs-advanced_features-hisparse_guide-why-hisparse*

In long-context LLM inference, each decoding request holds a full-length KV
cache on GPU, limiting the number of concurrent requests a decode instance
can serve. HiSparse addresses this by:

- Reducing GPU memory per request: Each request occupies only a fixed-size
  device buffer (e.g., 4KB tokens) instead of the full sequence length.
- On-demand swap-in: A CUDA kernel dynamically loads the top-k most relevant
  KV entries from host memory based on attention scores.
- Transparent to prefill: HiSparse is entirely a decode-side optimization;
  the prefill instance requires no changes.

DESIGN OVERVIEW        *docs-advanced_features-hisparse_guide-design-overview*

Decode Workflow        *docs-advanced_features-hisparse_guide-decode-workflow*

Each decode step follows this flow:

1. Forward decode --- generate the next token
2. Top-k selection --- select the most relevant token positions via
   attention scores
3. Swap-in --- the CUDA kernel loads top-k KV entries from host to device
   buffer:
   - Short sequences (`seq_len ≤ device_buffer_size`): fast path, all KV
     already in buffer
   - Long sequences: hit detection → LRU reordering → miss handling (host →
     device copy)
4. Decode attention --- compute attention using the top-k device locations
5. Eager backup --- asynchronously copy the previous token's KV from device
   to host

*docs-advanced_features-hisparse_guide-pd-disaggregation-integration-direct-to-host*
PD Disaggregation Integration (Direct-to-Host)

In PD disaggregation mode, the prefill instance transfers KV cache directly
into the decode instance's host pool via RDMA, bypassing the GPU entirely on
the decode side. This eliminates the transient GPU memory spike during KV
transfer and removes the staging DMA step.

>text
    Prefill GPU  ──RDMA──▶  Decode Host Pool (CPU pinned memory)
                                  │
                                  ▼
                         alloc device buffer (4KB)
                                  │
                                  ▼
                         swap-in kernel (on-demand top-k)
<
For DeepSeek V4, the direct-to-host path writes only C4 KV into the decode
host pool. The c4_indexer and C128 KV remain device-to-device transfers.

SERVER ARGUMENTS      *docs-advanced_features-hisparse_guide-server-arguments*

Argument          Type / Default           Description
----------------  -----------------------  -----------------------------------
---enable-hisparse  flag; default: disabled  Enable HiSparse on the decode
                                           instance
---hisparse-config  JSON string              Configuration for HiSparse (see
                                           below)

            *docs-advanced_features-hisparse_guide-hisparse-config-parameters*
HiSparse Config Parameters

Pass as a JSON string via `--hisparse-config`:

Parameter             Type / Default  Description
--------------------  --------------  ----------------------------------------
top_k                 int             Number of topk entries
device_buffer_size    int             Number of token slots in the per-request
                                      GPU device buffer
host_to_device_ratio  int             Ratio of logical pool size to device
                                      pool size, determining host memory
                                      capacity
swap_in_block_size    int / 960       CUDA thread-block size for the HiSparse
                                      swap-in kernel

Example:
`--hisparse-config='{"top_k": 2048, "device_buffer_size": 6144, "host_to_device_ratio": 10, "swap_in_block_size": 960}'`

       *docs-advanced_features-hisparse_guide-shared-index-prefetch-automatic*
Shared-index prefetch (automatic)

When a model reuses one anchor layer's top-k selection across a run of
subsequent “skip” layers (DSA `index_topk_freq` / `index_topk_pattern`;
native in GLM-5.2 as IndexShare), the working set of every skip layer is
known the moment the anchor's index is computed. HiSparse exploits this
automatically: the anchor's swap-in kernel records its miss plan (which host
slots go to which device-buffer slots), and each skip layer replays that
plan with a copy-only kernel issued ahead on a side stream, so the skip
layers' host→device IO overlaps the intervening layers' compute instead of
sitting on the decode critical path. The replay kernel uses a small fixed
grid to keep its SM footprint low while overlapped.

The prefetch is enabled automatically for eligible models (no pipeline
parallelism, no speculative decoding) and can be turned off for A/B
comparison with `SGLANG_DISABLE_HISPARSE_PREFETCH=1`.

DEPLOYMENT                  *docs-advanced_features-hisparse_guide-deployment*

HiSparse currently requires PD disaggregation mode and is enabled only on
the decode instance.

Prefill Instance      *docs-advanced_features-hisparse_guide-prefill-instance*

[Command]

[Command]Command

>sh
    python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
        --model-path /path/to/model \
        --trust-remote-code \
        --port 8000 --host 0.0.0.0 \
        --context-length 81920 \
        --chunked-prefill-size 65536 \
        --tp-size 8 --attn-dp-size 8 \
        --mem-fraction-static 0.85 \
        --disaggregation-mode prefill \
        --disaggregation-ib-device mlx5_0,mlx5_1,mlx5_2,mlx5_3 \
        --nnodes 1 --node-rank 0
<

         *docs-advanced_features-hisparse_guide-decode-instance-with-hisparse*
Decode Instance (with HiSparse)

[Command]

[Command]Command

>sh
    python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
        --model-path /path/to/model \
        --trust-remote-code \
        --port 8000 --host 0.0.0.0 \
        --context-length 81920 \
        --tp-size 8 --attn-dp-size 8 \
        --mem-fraction-static 0.85 \
        --disable-radix-cache \
        --disaggregation-mode decode \
        --disaggregation-ib-device mlx5_0,mlx5_1,mlx5_2,mlx5_3 \
        --dist-init-addr 127.0.0.1:5757 \
        --nnodes 1 --node-rank 0 \
        --enable-hisparse \
        --hisparse-config='{"top_k": 2048, "device_buffer_size": 6144, "host_to_device_ratio": 10, "swap_in_block_size": 960}'
<
  Note: For DSA models, `--kv-cache-dtype` defaults to `auto`, which
  resolves to `fp8_e4m3` on SM100+ (Blackwell) and on MI355X (gfx950) with
  AITER enabled and the `triton` or `tilelang` DSA backends, and `bfloat16`
  elsewhere. Pass `--kv-cache-dtype bfloat16` to keep a BF16 KV cache. The
  DSA decode backend is automatically selected based on KV dtype (`bfloat16`
  → `flashmla_sparse`, `fp8_e4m3` → `flashmla_kv`), except for GLM DSA
  models on SM120/SM121 with `fp8_e4m3`, which use `flashinfer_sparse_mla`.
  DSA backend flags apply only to DSA models; DeepSeek V4 uses its own
  `dsv4` attention backend.

MiniMax M3                  *docs-advanced_features-hisparse_guide-minimax-m3*

Dense-layer K/V and index K stay on GPU; sparse-layer K/V use host memory
plus a GPU working set.

- Use TP 4 or greater, with the same TP size and PP 1 on both PD instances.
- Use `--attention-backend triton`, `--mm-attention-backend triton_attn`,
  `--disable-prefill-cuda-graph`, and `--disable-radix-cache`.
- Set `device_buffer_size` to at least 2048 in `--hisparse-config`; `top_k`
  does not override the model's selection width.
- PD retraction backup is not supported. Use `--num-reserved-decode-tokens`
  to reserve capacity for the expected output length.

Kimi-K3.1                    *docs-advanced_features-hisparse_guide-kimi-k3-1*

Only the DSA layers use HiSparse; the KDA recurrent state stays on GPU and
is transferred as usual.

- Run the decode instance without `--dcp-size` and without
  `--disaggregation-decode-enable-radix-cache`; both are rejected with
  `--enable-hisparse`. The prefill instance must not use DCP either, since
  Mooncake cannot move KV from a DCP prefill to a non-DCP decode.
- The DSA backend resolves to `flashmla_kv`; `trtllm` is rejected.
- Use `--disaggregation-transfer-backend mooncake`. On hosts that mix
  InfiniBand and RoCE HCAs, list only one kind in
  `--disaggregation-ib-device`.
- DFLASH speculative decoding is supported up to block size 8 (`index_topk`
  2048 times 8 draft tokens is the 16384-occurrence limit of the speculative
  swap kernel).

Benchmark                    *docs-advanced_features-hisparse_guide-benchmark*

Key Notes                    *docs-advanced_features-hisparse_guide-key-notes*

- The prefill instance does not need `--enable-hisparse`; it is unaware of
  HiSparse.
- On the decode instance, `--enable-hisparse` and `--hisparse-config` are
  required for HiSparse.
- For DSA models, `--kv-cache-dtype bfloat16` uses `flashmla_sparse`, and
  `--kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3` uses `flashmla_kv`.
- On SM120/SM121 (e.g. RTX PRO 6000, RTX 5090) with GLM DSA models and
  `--kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3`, both DSA backends resolve to
  `flashinfer_sparse_mla`, which is the only DSA kernel available on that
  architecture. HiSparse accepts it there; no extra flag is needed.
- For DeepSeek V4, DSA backend flags are not applicable. DeepSeek V4 uses
  the `dsv4` attention backend and `fp8_e4m3` KV cache by default.
- `host_to_device_ratio` should be configured based on the host machine's
  available memory. For example:
  - ~1 TB host memory → `host_to_device_ratio: 5`
  - ~2 TB host memory → `host_to_device_ratio: 10`

----------------------------------------------------------------------------
                      *sglang-docs-advanced_features-hybrid_cache_checkpoints*
Hybrid Model Prefix-Cache Checkpoints

A hybrid model's linear-attention layers carry a recurrent state instead of
per-token KV. The prefix cache can reuse a cached prefix only up to a
position where it also kept that state, called a checkpoint.
`--hybrid-cache-checkpoints-level` decides where checkpoints are kept.

Level        Checkpoints                      Best for
-----------  -------------------------------  --------------------------------
2 (default)  Where two requests' prompts      Multi-turn chat, agents and tool
             diverge, and where each request  loops, where each request
             ends (on a PD prefill worker,    extends the previous one's full
             where its prompt ends). A soft   context.
             cap of one checkpoint per path,
             unless explicitly overridden.
3            Also every prefill chunk and     Traffic that reuses the middle
             every --mamba-track-interval     of an earlier prompt that no
             decode tokens.                   other request has diverged from
                                              yet.

The per-path cap is a pruning target, not a strict state-slot bound. Tail,
fork, locked, and device-leaf states can be preserved, so a path may retain
multiple checkpoints. Size the state pool for running requests and retained
checkpoints, and verify actual occupancy.

        *docs-advanced_features-hybrid_cache_checkpoints-what-level-2-changes*
WHAT LEVEL 2 CHANGES

- Request-end checkpoints support continued conversations. Level 2 preserves
  the checkpointing path used when the next turn extends the previous
  request's full context. Actual reuse still depends on checkpoint
  placement, KV and state capacity, eviction, and usable host backups; equal
  hit rates across levels are not guaranteed.
- Fewer intermediate checkpoints can reduce host and storage writes.
  HiCache, storage backends and the external linker receive published
  checkpoints, including fork and request-end states. Skipping intermediate
  checkpoints can reduce write traffic and pressure on other sessions'
  checkpoints; the benefit depends on the workload and cache configuration.
- A late fork may need more recomputation. If a request shares only the
  first part of an earlier prompt and lacks a matching checkpoint there, it
  resumes from the nearest usable earlier checkpoint, even if more KV is
  cached. Publishing a checkpoint at an eligible divergence point can help
  later siblings while that checkpoint and its KV remain available. Level 3
  offers more intermediate checkpoints, but does not guarantee a checkpoint
  at every possible divergence position.
- Ordinary requests defer intermediate cache publication. Away from fork
  points and the PD prefill exception, a prompt joins the tree at request
  finish rather than chunk by chunk, limiting sharing with concurrent
  requests during prefill.

Models with both sliding-window and linear-attention layers keep
checkpointing every prefill chunk at level 2.

MEASURED            *docs-advanced_features-hybrid_cache_checkpoints-measured*

These historical measurements from #49886
https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/49886 describe the listed models,
traffic, and cache configurations. They are examples, not a guarantee of
equal continuation hit rates, lower write traffic, or higher throughput.
Compare both continuation reuse and late-fork recomputation on your workload
before choosing a level.

Workload (B300)              Level 3                      Level 2
---------------------------  ---------------------------  --------------------
GLM-5.3-Flash, AgentX trace  0.943 / 42,741 (per-path     0.961 / 45,442
replay with HiCache: hit     cap set to 1)
rate / output tok/min/GPU
Qwen3.8-27B multi-turn       0.993 / 304 / 66.7 GB        0.993 / 87 / 33.4 GB
sessions with HiCache:
continuation hit / states
written to host / host
write bytes
Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, AgentX   0.961 / 59,480               0.960 / 60,525

             *docs-advanced_features-hybrid_cache_checkpoints-related-options*
RELATED OPTIONS

- `--mamba-max-states-per-path N` is deprecated. When set, it still sets the
  soft per-path cap at either level (`-1` means unlimited).
- The size of the state pool that holds the checkpoints is set by
  `--mamba-full-memory-ratio` or `--max-mamba-cache-size`; see
  |docs-advanced_features-server_arguments-mamba-cache|.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------
Hybrid Model Memory Pools  *sglang-docs-advanced_features-hybrid_model_memory*

Hybrid models mix full-attention layers with linear-attention layers (Mamba,
Gated DeltaNet, KDA). SGLang keeps two separate pools for them, sized once
at startup:

Pool        Holds                             Caps
----------  --------------------------------  --------------------------------
State pool  The recurrent state of each       Running concurrency and retained
            linear-attention layer: working   checkpoints. Idle sessions also
            states for running requests and   need a reusable checkpoint.
            checkpoints kept for prefix
            reuse.
KV pool     Full-attention KV, one row per    How many tokens are cached or in
            token.                            flight: running contexts plus
                                              the prefixes kept for reuse.

`--mamba-full-memory-ratio r` splits the memory left after weights: state
pool : KV pool = `r`. The default is `0.9`; some models override it (see
|docs-advanced_features-hybrid_model_memory-model-defaults|).
`--max-mamba-cache-size N` pins the state pool to `N` slots instead, and the
KV pool takes the rest.

 *docs-advanced_features-hybrid_model_memory-read-the-split-from-the-boot-log*
READ THE SPLIT FROM THE BOOT LOG

Each rank prints both pools:

>text
    Mamba Cache is allocated. max_mamba_cache_size: 429, conv_state size: 1.00GB, ssm_state size: 28.55GB
    KV Cache is allocated. dtype: torch.float8_e4m3fn, #tokens: 5890560, KV size: 32.89 GB
    max_running_requests is capped to 85 by the mamba state cache (max_mamba_cache_size=429, 5 state slots per request)
<
A running request holds several state slots: 5 with the default
`extra_buffer` strategy and the overlap scheduler, 4 with
`--mamba-radix-cache-strategy extra_buffer_lazy`, plus speculative draft
states. The last line appears when the state pool, not the KV pool, limits
concurrency.

              *docs-advanced_features-hybrid_model_memory-two-ways-to-run-out*
TWO WAYS TO RUN OUT

- Concurrency-bound (many short requests): the state pool fills first and
  caps `max_running_requests` while KV is idle. Raise the ratio or pin a
  larger `--max-mamba-cache-size`.
- Residency-bound (multi-turn chat, agents): sessions return turn after
  turn, and reuse requires both their KV prefixes and matching recurrent
  checkpoints. State eviction can prevent reuse even when all KV fits,
  unless a usable host backup remains. If KV is the bottleneck, lower the
  ratio only after checking state capacity for running requests and retained
  checkpoints. If checkpoints are the bottleneck, increase their capacity or
  use supported host backup; lowering the ratio can make reuse worse.

A KV residency cliff appeared in this GLM-5.3-Flash AgentX trace replay (48
total sessions, peak concurrency 48, median concurrency 27, TP2, pools fixed
at the same total memory):

State slots / KV tokens             Prefix-cache hit rate   Output throughput
----------------------------------  ----------------------  ------------------
429 / 5.89M (ratio 0.9)             0.06                    1x
300 / 7.48M                         0.22                    1.2x
192 / 8.81M (extra_buffer_lazy)     0.89                    4.8x

In this trace, the gap between peak and typical concurrency left space for
idle-session checkpoints. These results do not establish that the same
concurrency-based state budget is sufficient when sessions greatly outnumber
running requests.

SIZE THE POOLS     *docs-advanced_features-hybrid_model_memory-size-the-pools*

1. Estimate the peak number of running requests `R`, the per-request slot
   count `S` from the boot log, and how many sessions you want to retain
   between turns.
2. Budget state slots for the peak simultaneous running-state and
   retained-device-checkpoint demand, plus margin. Count checkpoints already
   included in the running-request budget only once. `S × R` plus margin is
   a concurrency starting point, not a guarantee of session residency.
3. Pin `--max-mamba-cache-size` to that state budget and check that the
   remaining KV pool's `#tokens` covers the retained sessions' total
   context. For concurrency-bound traffic, start from the balanced ratio the
   `compute-mamba-ratio`
   https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/.agents/skills/compute-mamba-ratio/SKILL.md
   skill computes from your average request length.
4. If you have safe memory headroom, consider raising
   `--mem-fraction-static`. Recheck both pool sizes; an explicitly pinned
   state-slot count stays fixed.
5. Verify on your traffic, including sessions far above concurrency: prefix
   reuse (`--enable-cache-report`, or `sglang:cached_tokens_total` with
   `--enable-metrics`), both pools' occupancy, and whether startup caps
   `max_running_requests`. Low active-state usage does not mean the state
   pool has room for more cached sessions.

For idle sessions, about one checkpoint per session is a starting estimate
with `--mamba-max-states-per-path 1`, not a strict upper bound. This is a
soft limit: tail, fork, locked, and device-leaf states can be preserved.
Allow margin and measure retained checkpoints. Account separately for usable
host backups and device space for restoring them.

The right ratio depends on the model and the deployment: it scales with the
size of one state slot relative to one KV token, with the context per
session and with the concurrency. Tuned values range from `0.1` to above
`1`. Do not copy a ratio between models.

MODEL DEFAULTS     *docs-advanced_features-hybrid_model_memory-model-defaults*

Model               Default                      Notes
------------------  ---------------------------  -----------------------------
Most hybrid models  0.9                          Generic starting point.
                                                 Cookbook recipes pass an
                                                 explicit value where it was
                                                 tuned.
Inkling             0.1
GLM-5.3-Flash       0.25 with extra_buffer_lazy  Sized for multi-turn agent
                                                 traffic. High Throughput
                                                 recipes on GPUs where it
                                                 would cap running requests
                                                 pin 0.9.

An explicit `--mamba-full-memory-ratio`, `--max-mamba-cache-size` or
`--mamba-radix-cache-strategy` always overrides the model default.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------
Hyperparameter Tuning    *sglang-docs-advanced_features-hyperparameter_tuning*

*docs-advanced_features-hyperparameter_tuning-achieving-high-throughput-for-offline-batch-inference*
ACHIEVING HIGH THROUGHPUT FOR OFFLINE BATCH INFERENCE

Achieving a large batch size is the most important thing for attaining high
throughput in offline batch inference. When the server is running at full
load in a steady state, look for the following in the log:

[Output]

[Output]Output

>text
    Decode batch. #running-req: 233, #token: 370959, token usage: 0.82, cuda graph: True, gen throughput (token/s): 4594.01, #queue-req: 317
<

*docs-advanced_features-hyperparameter_tuning-adjust-the-request-submission-speed-to-control-#queue-req*
Adjust the request submission speed to control `#queue-req`

`#queue-req` indicates the number of requests in the queue. If you
frequently see `#queue-req: 0`, it suggests that your client code is
submitting requests too slowly. A healthy range for `#queue-req` is
`100 - 2000`. However, avoid making `#queue-req` too large, as this will
increase the scheduling overhead on the server.

     *docs-advanced_features-hyperparameter_tuning-achieve-a-high-token-usage*
Achieve a high `token usage`

`token usage` indicates the KV cache memory utilization of the server.
`token usage > 0.9` means good utilization.

If you frequently see `token usage < 0.9` and `#queue-req > 0`, it means the
server is too conservative about taking in new requests. You can decrease
`--schedule-conservativeness` to a value like 0.3. The case of a server
being too conservative can happen when users send many requests with a large
`max_new_tokens` but the requests stop very early due to EOS or stop
strings.

On the other hand, if you see `token usage` very high and you frequently see
warnings like
`KV cache pool is full. Retract requests. #retracted_reqs: 1, #new_token_ratio: 0.9998 -> 1.0000`,
you can increase `--schedule-conservativeness` to a value like 1.3. If you
see `KV cache pool is full. Retract requests.` occasionally but not
frequently (~1 time per minute), it is okay.

*docs-advanced_features-hyperparameter_tuning-tune-mem-fraction-static-to-increase-kv-cache-pool-capacity*
Tune `--mem-fraction-static` to increase KV cache pool capacity

SGLang allocates memory as follows:

Total memory usage = model weights + KV cache pool + CUDA graph buffers +
activations

The `--mem-fraction-static` parameter determines how much memory is
allocated to the first two components:

mem_fraction_static = (model weights + KV cache pool) / GPU memory capacity

To support higher concurrency, you should maximize the KV cache pool
capacity by setting `--mem-fraction-static` as high as possible while still
reserving enough memory for activations and CUDA graph buffers.

SGLang uses simple heuristics to set the default value of
`--mem-fraction-static`, but you can optimize it for your use cases. As a
rule of thumb, reserving 5--8 GB of memory for activations is typically
sufficient. You can check this by inspecting the logs just before the server
is ready. Look for log entries like this:

[Output]

[Output]Output

>text
    [2025-08-11 17:17:03] max_total_num_tokens=665690, chunked_prefill_size=8192, max_prefill_tokens=16384, max_running_requests=4096, context_len=65536, available_gpu_mem=13.50 GB
<
Check the `available_gpu_mem` value.

- If it is between 5--8 GB, the setting is good.
- If it is too high (e.g., 10 - 20 GB), increase `--mem-fraction-static` to
  allocate more memory to the KV cache.
- If it is too low, you risk out-of-memory (OOM) errors later, so decrease
  `--mem-fraction-static`.

Another straightforward approach is to increase `--mem-fraction-static` in
increments of 0.01 until you encounter OOM errors for your workloads.

*docs-advanced_features-hyperparameter_tuning-avoid-out-of-memory-errors-by-tuning-chunked-prefill-size-mem-fraction-static-and-max-running-requests*
Avoid out-of-memory errors by tuning `--chunked-prefill-size`,
`--mem-fraction-static`, and `--max-running-requests`

If you encounter out-of-memory (OOM) errors, you can adjust the following
parameters:

- If OOM occurs during prefill, try reducing `--chunked-prefill-size` to
  `4096` or `2048`. This saves memory but slows down the prefill speed for
  long prompts.
- If OOM occurs during decoding, try lowering `--max-running-requests`.
- You can also reduce `--mem-fraction-static` to a smaller value, such as
  0.8 or 0.7. This decreases the memory usage of the KV cache memory pool
  and helps prevent OOM errors during both prefill and decoding. However, it
  limits maximum concurrency and reduces peak throughput.

  *docs-advanced_features-hyperparameter_tuning-tune-cuda-graph-max-bs-decode*
Tune `--cuda-graph-max-bs-decode`

By default, CUDA graph is enabled only for small batch sizes (e.g., less
than 160 or 256). However, for some models, especially at large tensor
parallelism sizes, CUDA graph can be useful for batch sizes up to 512 or
768. Therefore, it may be beneficial to increase
`--cuda-graph-max-bs-decode` to a larger value. Note that CUDA graph
consumes more memory, so you may need to reduce `--mem-fraction-static` at
the same time.

       *docs-advanced_features-hyperparameter_tuning-tune-dp-size-and-tp-size*
Tune `--dp-size` and `--tp-size`

Data parallelism is better for throughput. When there is enough GPU memory,
always favor data parallelism for throughput. Refer to
|sglang-docs-advanced_features-dp_dpa_router_guide| for a better data
parallelism with separate servers behind `sgl-router` rather than using
`dp_size` parameter.

              *docs-advanced_features-hyperparameter_tuning-try-other-options*
Try other options

- `torch.compile` accelerates small models on small batch sizes. You can
  enable it with `--enable-torch-compile`.
- Try other quantization (e.g. FP8 quantization with `--quantization fp8`)
- Try other parallelism strategies (e.g. expert parallelism
  https://lmsys.org/blog/2025-05-05-large-scale-ep/) or DP attention for
  deepseek models (with `--attn-dp-size 8`).
- If the workload has many shared prefixes, try `--schedule-policy lpm`.
  Here, `lpm` stands for longest prefix match. It reorders requests to
  encourage more cache hits but introduces more scheduling overhead.

  *docs-advanced_features-hyperparameter_tuning-lpm-under-long-waiting-queues*
LPM under long waiting queues

With prefix caching enabled, `lpm` keeps its existing matching and sorting
behavior for queues of at most 128 requests. Above 128, it checks the first
64 waiting requests for a prefix-reuse opportunity on the first eligible
scheduling pass and every 32 eligible passes thereafter. A pass is eligible
when the queue exceeds 128 and no committed batch remains. This
deterministic cadence keeps ranks sharing the queue independent of local
clock differences. The gate requires threatened reuse of at least 1.5 times
the KV capacity. Candidate requests are grouped by cache namespace and their
first 4096 tokens. Threatened reuse counts long shared prefixes whose
intervening unique input working set, including the reusable prefix, exceeds
the KV capacity. This is a heuristic input-based signal, not a guarantee of
cache savings or latency improvement. If the gate rejects, LPM retains its
FCFS fallback. Otherwise, it selects a fixed batch of up to 64 waiting
requests. Each pass rematches and reorders the remaining members. Members
are not replenished, and the batch finishes admission or cancellation before
the queue threshold is evaluated again.

Temporarily skipped members (prefetch, staging, LoRA availability, or
pooling compatibility) may allow one additional fixed batch of up to 64
requests to be attempted. Resource and budget breaks still end the pass.
This additional batch is never replenished while the current batch remains
active; its survivors are promoted when the current batch clears. All
committed batches must drain before short-queue LPM resumes. This bounds the
set of later requests considered during temporary blocking, not their
execution time.

The gate currently supports ordinary RadixCache and FULL-only
UnifiedRadixCache configurations. Hierarchical, session, sliding-window,
Mamba, and other unsupported cache modes retain the existing fallback.

Non-members retain the existing periodic, capped prefix refresh. dLLM
retains the original LPM large-queue FCFS fallback because its separate
transfer path does not use this admission loop. Disabling prefix caching
still uses FCFS. No new policy name or server argument is required.

*docs-advanced_features-hyperparameter_tuning-reduce-tail-latency-with-schedule-policy-uniboost*
Reduce tail latency with `--schedule-policy uniboost`

For mixed prompt lengths, such as agentic RL rollouts, `uniboost` admits
requests with little uncached prefill work ahead of long ones. Each request
gets a bounded boost, so long requests keep their place in line and are not
starved.

- `--uniboost-gamma` (default `10.0`) sets the boost decay rate. Lower
  values behave more like shortest-job-first; higher values behave more like
  `fcfs`.
- `--enable-uniboost-gamma-ada` tunes gamma online from the observed p95/p99
  latency, so you do not have to pick it per workload.
- With `--tp-size` or `--pp-size` above 1, a request's arrival is measured
  in prefill tokens processed before it was queued, not wall time, so every
  rank admits the same batch.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------
KV Cache Sharing              *sglang-docs-advanced_features-kv_cache_sharing*

KV cache sharing reduces duplicate KV storage across GPUs in a prefill
worker. It keeps one persistent copy of each cache page within the shard
group, allowing the same GPU memory budget to retain more unique tokens.

|sglang-docs-advanced_features-prefill_cp| distributes prompt computation,
but can still leave the cached history replicated across ranks. KV cache
sharing distributes those stored pages as well. This is useful for
long-context and multi-turn workloads that reuse large prefixes.

HOW IT WORKS            *docs-advanced_features-kv_cache_sharing-how-it-works*

*docs-advanced_features-kv_cache_sharing-shared-logical-tree-distributed-pages*
Shared logical tree, distributed pages

Every rank keeps the same logical radix tree and request-to-token mapping. A
prefix match therefore identifies the same cached tokens on all ranks, while
each GPU stores only the pages it owns.

For example, a CP4 group can distribute eight logical pages as follows:

Rank  Stored pages
----  ------------------------------------------------------------------------
0     A, E
1     B, F
2     C, G
3     D, H

A request that reuses A--D matches the same logical prefix on every rank.
New pages continue the cached path's ownership sequence, and prefixes remain
reusable at the original page size.

          *docs-advanced_features-kv_cache_sharing-gather-one-layer-at-a-time*
Gather one layer at a time

Before attention reads a cached prefix, each rank contributes its owned
pages to an all-gather. Attention reads the assembled prefix from a
temporary layer buffer, using a page-table mapping to preserve the logical
token order.

Two buffers alternate across layers so the next gather can overlap with
current-layer computation. Their memory is included in the cache budget. A
prefix hit saves recomputation, but still incurs the cost of gathering the
distributed KV.

         *docs-advanced_features-kv_cache_sharing-hicache-and-mtp-integration*
HiCache and MTP integration

|sglang-docs-advanced_features-hicache| preserves page ownership during
GPU-to-host backup and host-to-GPU reload. Each rank backs up and restores
its own pages. For each layer, execution follows this order:

[Read order]

[Read order]Read order

>text
    Restore local pages → Gather the prefix → Run attention
<
With GLM MTP, the target and draft KV/indexer state follow the same
ownership plan and are restored together. During
|sglang-docs-advanced_features-pd_disaggregation|, each prefill rank sends
the pages it owns; decode receives complete, unsharded cache entries.

USAGE EXAMPLE          *docs-advanced_features-kv_cache_sharing-usage-example*

Enable KV cache sharing with `--enable-kv-cache-sharding` on the prefill
worker only.

The following example uses Linux with NVIDIA CUDA on two GB300 nodes, with
four GPUs per worker. Prefill uses TP4/CP4 and CPU HiCache; decode uses
TP4/EP4 with attention DP4. Both workers use the same GLM-5.3 NVFP4
checkpoint and model revision.

               *docs-advanced_features-kv_cache_sharing-environment-variables*
Environment variables

Create `kv-shard.env` on both nodes. Replace the example IP addresses and
RDMA NIC names with values for your environment. This example uses Mooncake
RDMA for P/D transfer.

[Environment variables]

[Environment variables]Environment variables

>sh
    cat > kv-shard.env <<'EOF'
    export MODEL_PATH=RadixArk/GLM-5.3-NVFP4
    export MODEL_REVISION=6e389189d564d9d3e4ea7fa284fe91f136d8ae2a
    export PREFILL_HOST=192.0.2.10
    export DECODE_HOST=192.0.2.20
    export PREFILL_IB_DEVICES=mlx5_0,mlx5_1,mlx5_2,mlx5_3
    export DECODE_IB_DEVICES=mlx5_0,mlx5_1,mlx5_2,mlx5_3
    export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1,2,3
    export SGLANG_DISAGG_STAGING_BUFFER=0
    export MC_TCP_ENABLE_CONNECTION_POOL=true
    unset MC_FORCE_MNNVL SGLANG_MOONCAKE_CUSTOM_MEM_POOL
    EOF
<

              *docs-advanced_features-kv_cache_sharing-prefill-worker-tp4/cp4*
Prefill worker: TP4/CP4

KV sharding, CPU HiCache, and EAGLE MTP.

[Prefill worker]

llm-d                                    *sglang-docs-advanced_features-llm-d*

llm-d https://llm-d.ai/ is a Kubernetes-native distributed inference
framework for serving large language models at scale across a fleet of
inference servers. SGLang is a supported inference engine in llm-d: llm-d
coordinates a fleet of SGLang instances across a cluster so that performance
holds up under real production traffic, achieving the fastest “time to
state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance” for key OSS models across most hardware
accelerators.

llm-d is a CNCF Sandbox project
https://www.cncf.io/blog/2026/03/24/welcome-llm-d-to-the-cncf-evolving-kubernetes-into-sota-ai-infrastructure/
founded by Red Hat, Google Cloud, IBM Research, CoreWeave, and NVIDIA.

        *docs-advanced_features-llm-d-what-llm-d-adds-to-an-sglang-deployment*
WHAT LLM-D ADDS TO AN SGLANG DEPLOYMENT

A single SGLang server is fast, and RadixAttention already maximizes cache
reuse within each replica. But at scale the picture changes: across many
replicas, cache locality breaks under round-robin load balancing as related
requests scatter and radix-cache hit rates collapse, long prompts inflate
time-to-first-token, and accelerators sit underused. llm-d adds the
cluster-level layer that the engine does not aim to provide on its own:

- Prefix-aware routing
  https://llm-d.ai/docs/guides/precise-prefix-cache-aware. Instead of
  round-robin, the llm-d Router scores each replica on prefix-cache locality
  and current load, routing each request to the replica most likely to
  already hold its prefix --- raising RadixAttention hit rates on multi-turn
  and shared-prefix workloads while avoiding saturated servers.
- Distributed KV-cache management
  https://llm-d.ai/docs/guides#advanced-kv-cache-management. A global index
  tracks which token blocks live on which replica, and tiered offloading
  spills cache to CPU memory or local SSD, extending the working set beyond
  accelerator HBM.
- Prefill/decode disaggregation
  https://llm-d.ai/docs/guides/pd-disaggregation. Prompt processing and
  token generation run on separate workers, with KV-cache moved over
  high-speed interconnects, lowering TTFT and steadying per-token latency on
  long prompts.
- SLO-aware autoscaling https://llm-d.ai/docs/guides/workload-autoscaling
  and flow control https://llm-d.ai/docs/guides/flow-control. Scale SGLang
  pools on real inference signals (queue depth, true demand) rather than raw
  GPU utilization, with multi-tenant fairness and priority dispatch.
- One control plane for mixed fleets. llm-d schedules across engines, so
  platform teams can serve SGLang and vLLM pools behind the same gateway,
  policies, and observability instead of running parallel stacks.

These capabilities are composable. Most teams start by adding prefix-aware
routing over an existing SGLang pool, then layer in the rest as specific
bottlenecks appear.

                      *docs-advanced_features-llm-d-kubernetes-native-gateway*
KUBERNETES-NATIVE GATEWAY

llm-d builds on the Gateway API Inference Extension, so SGLang pools are
managed through standard Kubernetes resources (Gateway, HTTPRoute,
InferencePool) and work with supported gateway providers such as Istio, GKE
Inference Gateway, and agentgateway, rather than a bespoke routing tier.

PERFORMANCE                         *docs-advanced_features-llm-d-performance*

llm-d publishes reproducible benchmarks from production-scale deployments on
Prism https://prism.llm-d.ai/. One representative result: prefix-aware
routing delivered 3x higher output throughput and 2x faster TTFT than
round-robin load balancing (Llama 3.1 70B). The mechanism carries over
directly to SGLang, where RadixAttention makes the cluster-level cache hit
rate a function of routing.

GET STARTED                         *docs-advanced_features-llm-d-get-started*

- Deploy the optimized baseline with the Quickstart
  https://llm-d.ai/docs/getting-started/quickstart, selecting SGLang as the
  inference server. It stands up an intelligent router (the llm-d Router)
  over an SGLang pool on Kubernetes in a tested configuration.
- Browse the well-lit path guides https://llm-d.ai/docs/guides, each a
  tested recipe for one of the capabilities above, and add the optimization
  that fits your workload.
- Read the Introduction https://llm-d.ai/docs/getting-started and
  Architecture overview https://llm-d.ai/docs/architecture to see how the
  scheduler, gateway, and model servers wrap your SGLang deployment.

Questions and contributions are welcome on GitHub
https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d and Slack https://llm-d.ai/slack.

CURRENT SCOPE                     *docs-advanced_features-llm-d-current-scope*

SGLang is supported across the well-lit paths --- including intelligent
inference scheduling, precise prefix-cache routing (SGLang publishes
KV-cache events that the llm-d Router subscribes to), tiered KV-cache
management, prefill/decode disaggregation, flow control, and autoscaling.
The one current exception is Multi-Node Wide Expert Parallelism, which is
vLLM-specific today. See the llm-d documentation for the latest per-engine
support status.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------
LoRA Serving                              *sglang-docs-advanced_features-lora*

SGLang enables the use of LoRA adapters https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685
with a base model. By incorporating techniques from S-LoRA
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.03285 and Punica
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.18547, SGLang can efficiently support multiple
LoRA adapters for different sequences within a single batch of inputs.

                      *docs-advanced_features-lora-arguments-for-lora-serving*
ARGUMENTS FOR LORA SERVING

The following server arguments are relevant for multi-LoRA serving:

- `enable_lora`: Enable LoRA support for the model. This argument is
  automatically set to True if `--lora-paths` is provided for backward
  compatibility.
- `enable_lora_overlap_loading`: Enable asynchronous LoRA weight loading in
  order to overlap H2D transfers with GPU compute. This should be enabled if
  you find that your LoRA workloads are bottlenecked by adapter weight
  loading, for example when frequently loading large LoRA adapters.
- `lora_paths`: The list of LoRA adapters to load. Each adapter must be
  specified in one of the following formats: <PATH> | <NAME>=<PATH> | JSON
  with schema {“lora_name”:str,“lora_path”:str,“pinned”:bool}.
- `max_loras_per_batch`: GPU pool capacity in distinct adapter IDs,
  including `None` for base-model requests. With pipeline parallelism, this
  capacity is shared across all in-flight microbatches. More slots reserve
  more GPU memory. Defaults to 8.
- `max_loaded_loras`: If specified, it limits the maximum number of LoRA
  adapters loaded in CPU memory at a time. The value must be greater than or
  equal to `max-loras-per-batch`.
- `lora_eviction_policy`: LoRA adapter eviction policy when GPU memory pool
  is full. `lru`: Least Recently Used (default, better cache efficiency).
  `fifo`: First-In-First-Out.
- `lora_backend`: The backend of running GEMM kernels for Lora modules.
  Currently we support Triton LoRA backend (`triton`) and Chunked SGMV
  backend (`csgmv`). In the future, faster backend built upon Cutlass or
  Cuda kernels will be added.
- `max_lora_rank`: The maximum LoRA rank that should be supported. If not
  specified, it will be automatically inferred from the adapters provided in
  `--lora-paths`. This argument is needed when you expect to dynamically
  load adapters of larger LoRA rank after server startup.
- `lora_target_modules`: The union set of all target modules where LoRA
  should be applied (e.g., `q_proj`, `k_proj`, `gate_proj`). If not
  specified, it will be automatically inferred from the adapters provided in
  `--lora-paths`. This argument is needed when you expect to dynamically
  load adapters of different target modules after server startup. You can
  also set it to `all` to enable LoRA for all supported modules. However,
  enabling LoRA on additional modules introduces a minor performance
  overhead. If your application is performance-sensitive, we recommend only
  specifying the modules for which you plan to load adapters.
- `max_lora_chunk_size`: Maximum chunk size for the ChunkedSGMV LoRA
  backend. Only used when ---lora-backend is ‘csgmv'. Choosing a larger
  value might improve performance. Please tune this value based on your
  hardware and workload as needed. Defaults to 16.
- `lora_drain_wait_threshold`: Once an adapter's oldest waiting request
  exceeds this threshold (seconds), the scheduler can drain an unpinned
  running adapter to make room. Multiple adapters can be drained when
  several waiting adapters need slots. Each drain limits new requests to a
  fixed running request's remaining output budget. Pinned adapters are never
  drained. This is best effort: the threshold starts draining without
  reserving a freed slot or guaranteeing a maximum waiting time. Set to 0 to
  disable draining (default).
- `tp_size`: LoRA serving along with Tensor Parallelism is supported by
  SGLang. `tp_size` controls the number of GPUs for tensor parallelism. More
  details on the tensor sharding strategy can be found in S-Lora
  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.03285 paper.

From client side, the user needs to provide a list of strings as input
batch, and a list of adaptor names that each input sequence corresponds to.

USAGE                                      *docs-advanced_features-lora-usage*

Serving Single Adaptor    *docs-advanced_features-lora-serving-single-adaptor*

1. OpenAI-Compatible API (`/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/completions`): Use
   the `model:adapter-name` syntax. See

   examples.
2. Native API (`/generate`): Pass `lora_path` in the request body (shown
   below).

Dynamic LoRA loading        *docs-advanced_features-lora-dynamic-lora-loading*

Instead of specifying all adapters during server startup via `--lora-paths`.
You can also load & unload LoRA adapters dynamically via the
`/load_lora_adapter` and `/unload_lora_adapter` API.

Both are admin endpoints: launch the server with
`SGLANG_ADMIN_API_KEY=<key>` set (or pass `--admin-api-key <key>`) and send
`Authorization: Bearer <key>` with each call. Without an admin key
configured, the server answers HTTP 403 (`--api-key` does not unlock them).

When using dynamic LoRA loading, it's recommended to explicitly specify both
`--max-lora-rank` and `--lora-target-modules` at startup. For backward
compatibility, SGLang will infer these values from `--lora-paths` if they
are not explicitly provided. However, in that case, you would have to ensure
that all dynamically loaded adapters share the same shape (rank and target
modules) as those in the initial `--lora-paths` or are strictly “smaller”.

[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    import os

    lora0 = "Nutanix/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct_SFT_lora_4_alpha_16_humaneval_raw_json"  # rank - 4, target modules - q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, o_proj, gate_proj
    lora1 = "algoprog/fact-generation-llama-3.1-8b-instruct-lora"  # rank - 64, target modules - q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, o_proj, gate_proj, up_proj, down_proj
    lora0_new = "philschmid/code-llama-3-1-8b-text-to-sql-lora"  # rank - 256, target modules - q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, o_proj, gate_proj, up_proj, down_proj


    # The `--lora-target-modules` param below is technically not needed, as the server will infer it from lora0 which already has all the target modules specified.
    # We are adding it here just to demonstrate usage.
    os.environ["SGLANG_ADMIN_API_KEY"] = "your-admin-api-key"
    server_process, port = launch_server_cmd(
        """
        python3 -m sglang.launch_server --model-path meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct \
        --enable-lora \
        --cuda-graph-max-bs-decode 2 \
        --max-loras-per-batch 2 \
        --max-lora-rank 256
        --lora-target-modules all
        --log-level warning
        """
    )

    url = f"http://127.0.0.1:{port}"
    wait_for_server(url)

    admin_headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['SGLANG_ADMIN_API_KEY']}"}

                     *docs-advanced_features-lora-openai-compatible-api-usage*
OpenAI-compatible API usage

You can use LoRA adapters via the OpenAI-compatible APIs by specifying the
adapter in the `model` field using the `base-model:adapter-name` syntax (for
example, `qwen/qwen2.5-0.5b-instruct:adapter_a`). For more details and
examples, see the “Using LoRA Adapters” section in the OpenAI API
documentation: |sglang-docs-basic_usage-openai_api_completions|.

LoRA GPU Pinning                *docs-advanced_features-lora-lora-gpu-pinning*

Another advanced option is to specify adapters as `pinned` during loading.
When an adapter is pinned, it is permanently assigned to one of the
available GPU pool slots (as configured by `--max-loras-per-batch`) and will
not be evicted from GPU memory during runtime. Instead, it remains resident
until it is explicitly unloaded.

This can improve performance in scenarios where the same adapter is
frequently used across requests, by avoiding repeated memory transfers and
reinitialization overhead. However, since GPU pool slots are limited,
pinning adapters reduces the flexibility of the system to dynamically load
other adapters on demand. If too many adapters are pinned, it may lead to
degraded performance, or in the most extreme case
(`Number of pinned adapters == max-loras-per-batch`), halt all unpinned
requests. Therefore, currently SGLang limits maximal number of pinned
adapters to `max-loras-per-batch - 1` to prevent unexpected starvations.

In the example below, we start a server with `lora1` loaded as pinned,
`lora2` and `lora3` loaded as regular (unpinned) adapters. Please note that,
we intentionally specify `lora2` and `lora3` in two different formats to
demonstrate that both are supported.

[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    server_process, port = launch_server_cmd(
        """
        python3 -m sglang.launch_server --model-path meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct \
        --enable-lora \
        --cuda-graph-max-bs-decode 8 \
        --max-loras-per-batch 3 \
        --max-lora-rank 256 \
        --lora-target-modules all \
        --lora-paths \
            {"lora_name":"lora0","lora_path":"Nutanix/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct_SFT_lora_4_alpha_16_humaneval_raw_json","pinned":true} \
            {"lora_name":"lora1","lora_path":"algoprog/fact-generation-llama-3.1-8b-instruct-lora"} \
            lora2=philschmid/code-llama-3-1-8b-text-to-sql-lora
        --log-level warning
        """
    )


    url = f"http://127.0.0.1:{port}"
    wait_for_server(url)
<
You can also specify adapter as pinned during dynamic adapter loading. In
the example below, we reload `lora2` as pinned adapter:

CHOOSING LORA BACKEND      *docs-advanced_features-lora-choosing-lora-backend*

SGLang supports two LoRA backends that you can choose from using the
`--lora-backend` argument:

- `triton`: Basic Triton-based backend.
- `csgmv`: Default chunked SGMV backend optimized for high concurrency
  scenarios.

The `csgmv` backend was recently introduced to improve performance
especially at high-concurrency scenarios. Our benchmark shows that it
achieves 20% to 80% latency improvements over the basic triton backend.

[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    server_process, port = launch_server_cmd(
        """
        python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
        --model-path meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct \
        --enable-lora \
        --lora-backend csgmv \
        --max-loras-per-batch 16 \
        --lora-paths lora1=path/to/lora1 lora2=path/to/lora2
        """
    )
<

[Example]Example

>python

                  *docs-advanced_features-lora-lora-with-pipeline-parallelism*
LORA WITH PIPELINE PARALLELISM

With `--pp-size > 1`, each stage shares its LoRA GPU pool across all
in-flight microbatches. `--max-loras-per-batch` limits the union of their
adapter IDs, including one slot for `None` when base-model requests are
present.

Each stage allocates transformer-layer LoRA buffers only for its local
modules. For balanced partitions of homogeneous layers at the same slot
count and LoRA rank, these buffers use approximately `1 / pp_size` of their
unpartitioned size per stage. Embedding and output-head buffers follow the
LoRA-enabled modules present on each stage. This ratio does not describe
total GPU memory usage. You can increase `--max-loras-per-batch` if your
actual GPU memory budget permits.

When requests target more adapters than fit in the pool, requests for
additional adapters wait for a slot. To improve fairness under skewed
traffic, set |docs-advanced_features-lora-arguments-for-lora-serving| to a
positive value. Its default, `0`, disables draining.

LORA WITH DP ATTENTION    *docs-advanced_features-lora-lora-with-dp-attention*

SGLang supports LoRA serving with
|sglang-docs-advanced_features-dp_dpa_router_guide|. The model architecture
must support DPA, and you must currently select the Triton LoRA backend.
Other built-in LoRA backends reject this configuration at startup.

The following NVIDIA CUDA example uses four attention-DP ranks:

>sh
    python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
        --model-path MODEL_PATH \
        --tp 4 \
        --attn-dp-size 4 \
        --enable-lora \
        --lora-backend triton \
        --lora-paths '{"lora_name":"ADAPTER_NAME","lora_path":"ADAPTER_PATH","pinned":true}'
<
Keep these constraints in mind:

- `--attn-dp-size` must equal `--tp-size`, so every attention DP rank owns
  its whole token batch. The server rejects other layouts at startup.
- All adapters must be GPU-pinned (`pinned: true`), including dynamically
  loaded adapters. You can pin at most `--max-loras-per-batch - 1` adapters;
  the remaining slot is reserved for the base model.
- Decode CUDA graphs are supported. LoRA prefill runs eagerly when DPA is
  enabled.
- `--max-loras-per-batch` limits the union of adapters active across all DP
  ranks in a synchronized forward, not the adapters on one rank alone.
- Dynamic load and unload requests are sent to every DP rank. An operation
  succeeds only if every rank reports success. After a partially successful
  load, retry unloading the same adapter name before loading it again.
- The built-in LoRA memory pool does not support
  `--enable-lora-overlap-loading` with DPA. The server rejects that
  combination rather than allowing DP ranks to assign different GPU slots.

LORA OVERLAP LOADING        *docs-advanced_features-lora-lora-overlap-loading*

By using the `--enable-lora-overlap-loading` server argument, the SGLang
engine is able to overlap the loading of LoRA weights with prefill and
decode compute, essentially hiding the data movement for LoRA weights behind
GPU computation. Our benchmarks show that under adversarial conditions,
enabling this feature can result in a ~35% reduction in median TTFT - (see
the LoRA overlap loading PR https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/15512
for detailed benchmarks).

[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    lora0 = "Nutanix/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct_SFT_lora_4_alpha_16_humaneval_raw_json"
    lora1 = "algoprog/fact-generation-llama-3.1-8b-instruct-lora"
    lora2 = "philschmid/code-llama-3-1-8b-text-to-sql-lora"


    server_process, port = launch_server_cmd(
        """
        python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
        --model-path meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct \
        --enable-lora \
        --enable-lora-overlap-loading \
        --lora-paths lora0=Nutanix/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct_SFT_lora_4_alpha_16_humaneval_raw_json \
        lora1=algoprog/fact-generation-llama-3.1-8b-instruct-lora \
        lora2=philschmid/code-llama-3-1-8b-text-to-sql-lora \
        --max-lora-rank 256 \
        --max-loras-per-batch 2 \
        --max-loaded-loras 4
        """
    )

    url = f"http://127.0.0.1:{port}"
    wait_for_server(url)
<
[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    json_data = {
        "text": [
            "Write a very long fairy-tale.",
            "List 3 countries and their capitals.",
            "List 3 countries and their capitals.",
        ],
        "sampling_params": [
            {"max_new_tokens": 1024, "temperature": 0},
            {"max_new_tokens": 64, "temperature": 0},
            {"max_new_tokens": 64, "temperature": 0},
        ],
        "lora_path": ["lora0", "lora1", "lora2"],
    }

    # lora0 and lora1 will be loaded into the memory pool first, and because max_loras_per_batch = 2, lora2's request will remain in the queue.
    # lora1's request will likely finish first, and once it does, lora2 will be loaded. With --enable-lora-overlap-loading, this loading will
    # occur asynchronously and thus decoding for lora0's request won't be blocked.
    response = requests.post(
        url + "/generate",
        json=json_data,
    )

    for i in range(3):
        print(f"Output from lora{i}: \n{response.json()[i]['text']}\n")

[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    terminate_process(server_process)
<

             *docs-advanced_features-lora-limitations-of-lora-overlap-loading*
Limitations of LoRA Overlap Loading

However, LoRA overlap loading is not free and comes with two important
caveats:

1. Pinned CPU memory requirement: Asynchronous H2D memory copies require
   LoRA weights to be pinned in CPU memory, which is a finite system
   resource. To mitigate excessive pinned-memory usage, SGLang currently
   restricts `max_loaded_loras` to be at most 2× `max_loras_per_batch` when
   LoRA overlap loading is enabled.
2. Reduced multi-adapter prefill batching: With overlap loading, adapters
   become available on the GPU at different times because each adapter is
   loaded asynchronously. This can reduce the scheduler's ability to form
   multi-adapter prefill batches, since only requests whose adapters are
   currently loaded can be grouped together. As a result, requests for
   different adapters will be scheduled in separate (or smaller) prefill
   batches, which can increase TTFT when adapter load time is small compared
   to prefill compute time. This is why LoRA overlap loading is disabled by
   default: it should only be enabled when users have determined that LoRA
   weight loading is a bottleneck (EG high adapter churn, heavy adapter
   weights, or PCIe-bottlenecked workloads).

*docs-advanced_features-lora-example-when-overlap-loading-results-in-higher-latency*
Example When Overlap Loading Results in Higher Latency

For instance, suppose we have four LoRA adapters: `lora0`, `lora1`, `lora2`,
and `lora3`. Loading any adapter takes 2ms, while the prefill step for
requests for that adapter takes 20ms.

1. Baseline: The engine loads all four adapters synchronously, then runs one
   combined prefill batch, giving us a total time of ≈ `2 * 4 + 20 = 28ms`
2. With LoRA overlap loading enabled: The engine begins loading `lora0` and,
   once it is ready, schedules a prefill batch containing only `lora0` while
   `lora1` loads in the background. Then it schedules `lora1`'s prefill
   while `lora2` loads, and so on. In the worst case where prefill cannot be
   batched across adapters, total time is ≈ `2 + 4 * 20 = 82ms`

In this scenario, overlap loading reduces adapter-load overhead, but the
loss of multi-adapter prefill batching dominates and leads to higher TTFT.

FUTURE WORKS                        *docs-advanced_features-lora-future-works*

The development roadmap for LoRA-related features can be found in this issue
https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/2929. Other features, including
Embedding Layer, Unified Paging, Cutlass backend are still under
development.

Model Loading                    *sglang-docs-advanced_features-model_loading*

Control how SGLang loads model weights: load formats, model loader extra
config, multithreaded loading, prefetching, and remote/streaming loaders.

`--model-path` selects the checkpoint to serve; `--load-format` and the
weight-loading flags below control how those weights are read into memory.
To stream weights from cloud object storage (S3/GCS/Azure), see
|sglang-docs-advanced_features-object_storage|.

HOW LOADING WORKS     *docs-advanced_features-model_loading-how-loading-works*

SGLang picks a loader from `--load-format`, falling back to auto-detection
from the checkpoint or model path. The default `auto` loader reads
`safetensors` and falls back to PyTorch `.bin`.

>sh
    python -m sglang.launch_server \
      --model-path Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B \
      --load-format auto
<
Some formats are auto-detected and override `auto`:

- A Mistral native checkpoint is detected and loaded with `mistral`.
- A `.gguf` model path is detected and loaded with `gguf`.
- An object storage URI (`s3://`, `gs://`, `az://`) is loaded with
  `runai_streamer`.
- A remote URI is loaded with `remote`.

LOAD FORMATS               *docs-advanced_features-model_loading-load-formats*

Set with `--load-format`:

Format           Description
---------------  -------------------------------------------------------------
auto             Default. Load safetensors if available, otherwise fall back
                 to the PyTorch .bin format.
safetensors      Load weights in the safetensors format.
instanttensor    Load Safetensors weights quickly with InstantTensor's
                 distributed loading and pipelined prefetching. Supports CUDA
                 and ROCm; requires PyTorch's cuda device interface.
                 Distributed loading may retain communicator memory for the
                 server lifetime.
pt               Load weights in the PyTorch .bin format.
npcache          Load PyTorch-format weights and store a numpy cache to speed
                 up subsequent loads. Only supports .bin checkpoints.
dummy            Initialize weights with random values, for profiling.
sharded_state    Each tensor-parallel worker reads only its own pre-sharded
                 shard rather than the full checkpoint, giving a fast load
                 path for large TP models. See
                 examples/runtime/engine/save_sharded_state.py for creating a
                 sharded checkpoint.
fastsafetensors  Load safetensors using the fastsafetensors iterator.
layered          Load weights layer by layer, so a layer can be quantized
                 before the next is loaded, lowering the peak memory envelope.
gguf             Load weights in the GGUF format. Auto-detected from a .gguf
                 model path.
bitsandbytes     Load weights using bitsandbytes quantization.
mistral          Load a Mistral native-format checkpoint. Auto-detected for
                 such checkpoints.
flash_rl         Load a BF16/FP16 checkpoint with native SGLang FP8
                 quantization for RL training. Requires ---rl-quant-profile.
runai_streamer   Stream weights from SSDs, shared filesystems, or object
                 storage. See Loading Models from Object Storage.
remote           Load tensors from a remote KV/filesystem connector.
                 Auto-detected for remote URIs.
remote_instance  Pull weights over the network from another running SGLang
                 instance (the “seed”) rather than from disk. Configured with
                 the ---remote-instance-weight-loader-* flags.

                                *sglang-docs-advanced_features-object_storage*
Loading Models from Object Storage

SGLang can load models directly from object storage without a full local
download. It uses the `runai_streamer` load format to stream model weights
from cloud storage, reducing startup time and local storage requirements.

OVERVIEW                      *docs-advanced_features-object_storage-overview*

When loading models from object storage, SGLang uses a two-phase approach:

1. Metadata Download (once, before process launch): Configuration files and
   tokenizer files are downloaded to a local cache
2. Weight Streaming (lazy, during model loading): Model weights are streamed
   directly from object storage as needed

            *docs-advanced_features-object_storage-supported-storage-backends*
SUPPORTED STORAGE BACKENDS

1. Amazon S3: `s3://bucket-name/path/to/model/`
2. Google Cloud Storage: `gs://bucket-name/path/to/model/`
3. Azure Blob: `az://some-azure-container/path/`
4. S3 compatible: `s3://bucket-name/path/to/model/`

QUICK START                *docs-advanced_features-object_storage-quick-start*

Basic Usage                *docs-advanced_features-object_storage-basic-usage*

Simply provide an object storage URI as the model path:

>sh
    # S3
    python -m sglang.launch_server \
      --model-path s3://my-bucket/models/llama-3-8b/ \
      --load-format runai_streamer

    # Google Cloud Storage
    python -m sglang.launch_server \
      --model-path gs://my-bucket/models/llama-3-8b/ \
      --load-format runai_streamer
<
Note: The `--load-format runai_streamer` is automatically detected when
using object storage URIs, so you can omit it:

>sh
    python -m sglang.launch_server \
      --model-path s3://my-bucket/models/llama-3-8b/
<

               *docs-advanced_features-object_storage-with-tensor-parallelism*
With Tensor Parallelism

>sh
    python -m sglang.launch_server \
      --model-path gs://my-bucket/models/llama-70b/ \
      --tp 4 \
      --model-loader-extra-config '{"distributed": true}'
<

CONFIGURATION            *docs-advanced_features-object_storage-configuration*

Load Format                *docs-advanced_features-object_storage-load-format*

The `runai_streamer` load format is designed for object storage, SSDs, and
shared filesystems.

>sh
    python -m sglang.launch_server \
      --model-path s3://bucket/model/ \
      --load-format runai_streamer
<

     *docs-advanced_features-object_storage-extended-configuration-parameters*
Extended Configuration Parameters

Use `--model-loader-extra-config` to pass additional configuration as a JSON
string:

>sh
    python -m sglang.launch_server \
      --model-path s3://bucket/model/ \
      --model-loader-extra-config '{
        "distributed": true,
        "concurrency": 8,
        "memory_limit": 2147483648
      }'
<

                  *docs-advanced_features-object_storage-available-parameters*
Available Parameters

Parameter     Type  Description                               Default
------------  ----  ----------------------------------------  ----------------
distributed   bool  Enable distributed streaming for          Auto-detected
                    multi-GPU setups. Automatically set to
                    true for object storage paths on
                    CUDA-like devices.
concurrency   int   Number of concurrent download streams.    4
                    Higher values can improve throughput for
                    large models.
memory_limit  int   Memory limit (in bytes) for the           System-dependent
                    streaming buffer.

            *docs-advanced_features-object_storage-performance-considerations*
PERFORMANCE CONSIDERATIONS

                 *docs-advanced_features-object_storage-distributed-streaming*
Distributed Streaming

For multi-GPU setups, enable distributed streaming to parallelize weight
loading across processes:

>sh
    python -m sglang.launch_server \
      --model-path s3://bucket/model/ \
      --tp 8 \
      --model-loader-extra-config '{"distributed": true}'
<

LIMITATIONS                *docs-advanced_features-object_storage-limitations*

- Supported formats: Only the `.safetensors` weight format is supported.
- Supported devices: Distributed streaming is supported on CUDA-like
  devices; otherwise it falls back to non-distributed streaming.

PRODUCTION METRICS   *docs-advanced_features-observability-production-metrics*

SGLang exposes the following metrics via Prometheus. You can enable them by
adding `--enable-metrics` when launching the server. You can query them by:

[Command]

[Command]Command

>sh
    curl http://localhost:30000/metrics
<
See |sglang-docs-references-production_metrics| and
|sglang-docs-references-production_request_trace| for more details.

LOGGING                         *docs-advanced_features-observability-logging*

By default, SGLang does not log any request contents. You can log them by
using `--log-requests`. You can control the verbosity by using
`--log-requests-level`. See
|docs-advanced_features-server_arguments-logging| for more details.

You can change verbosity at runtime. `/configure_logging` is an admin
endpoint, so the server must be launched with `SGLANG_ADMIN_API_KEY` set (or
`--admin-api-key`), and the tool reads the same key from
`SGLANG_ADMIN_API_KEY`:

[Command]

[Command]Command

>sh
    python3 -m sglang.srt.managers.configure_logging --url http://localhost:30000 --log-level=debug
<

                *docs-advanced_features-observability-request-dump-and-replay*
REQUEST DUMP AND REPLAY

You can dump all requests and replay them later for benchmarking or other
purposes.

To start dumping, use the following command to send a request to a server:

[Command]

[Command]Command

>sh
    python3 -m sglang.srt.managers.configure_logging --url http://localhost:30000 --dump-requests-folder /tmp/sglang_request_dump --dump-requests-threshold 100
<
The server will dump the requests into a pickle file for every 100 requests.

To replay the request dump, use `scripts/playground/replay_request_dump.py`.

                  *docs-advanced_features-observability-crash-dump-and-replay*
CRASH DUMP AND REPLAY

Sometimes the server might crash, and you may want to debug the cause of the
crash. SGLang can preserve recent request data for replay and collect CUDA
device coredumps for low-level debugging.

Set the crash diagnostics folder with `--crash-dump-folder /tmp/crash_dump`.

When SGLang handles a crash, it writes completed requests retained by the
crash-dump buffer plus in-flight requests to
`/tmp/crash_dump/<hostname>/crash_dump_<timestamp>.pkl`. The file also
contains the server arguments and launch command. Replay it with
`scripts/playground/replay_request_dump.py`.

On NVIDIA CUDA, the option also sets default environment variables before
CUDA initializes. These defaults enable device coredumps on CUDA exceptions
and allow SGLang to trigger device coredumps for live scheduler processes
when it handles a crash. CUDA device coredumps are written to
`/tmp/crash_dump/<hostname>/core.cuda.<timestamp>.<pid>`. Explicitly
configured CUDA coredump environment variables take precedence, including a
custom `CUDA_COREDUMP_FILE` path. This option does not configure OS process
core dumps.
