Paged Experts                    *sglang-docs-advanced_features-paged_experts*

Paged Experts serves a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model whose expert weights
do not fit in GPU memory. Each MoE layer keeps K of its E routed experts in
a K-slot table on the GPU and holds all E experts in pinned host memory;
every step, the experts the step routes to that are not resident are copied
into slots before the expert GEMM runs.

WHY PAGED EXPERTS?    *docs-advanced_features-paged_experts-why-paged-experts*

Expert weights are most of an MoE model's parameters, yet each token is
routed to only `top_k` of the `E` experts per layer, and consecutive tokens
reuse many of the same experts. Paged Experts keeps a working set of K
experts per layer resident and pages the rest in from host memory as routing
requires them, so expert capacity is bounded by host RAM rather than VRAM.

Computation stays on the GPU. Only expert storage is host-backed: experts
are copied to the GPU and computed there by the model's own fused-MoE
kernel. This differs from `--cpu-offload-gb` and CPU expert offload, which
move the computation to the CPU.

Results are unchanged. Routing is untouched (E-wide), and the paged layer
produces the same output as the unpaged one: bit-identical for unquantized,
FP8 and INT8 experts (with `--enable-deterministic-inference`), and within
the Marlin kernel's own run-to-run noise for the other quantized formats.
See |docs-advanced_features-paged_experts-correctness|.

USAGE                             *docs-advanced_features-paged_experts-usage*

>sh
    python -m sglang.launch_server \
      --model-path Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-GPTQ-Int4 \
      --enable-paged-experts
<
At startup the KV cache keeps room for one request of the model's context,
and the rest of the static memory holds as many experts per layer (K) as
fit; the log names the K it chose and what would change it. See
|docs-advanced_features-paged_experts-choosing-k| to trade context or
concurrency for resident experts, or to set K yourself.

The default CUDA graphs stay on: decode graphs are captured up to
`K // top_k` concurrent requests, and breakable prefill graphs run the paged
MoE layers as eager breaks.

RELATED PARAMETERS   *docs-advanced_features-paged_experts-related-parameters*

- `--enable-paged-experts`: Enable Paged Experts. Off by default.
- `--paged-experts-num-resident K|auto`: Routed experts per MoE layer kept
  on the GPU, at least the router's `top_k`; larger values page less but
  leave less memory for the KV cache. `auto` (the default) sizes K after the
  model is loaded; see |docs-advanced_features-paged_experts-choosing-k|.
- `--paged-experts-enable-disk`: Let Paged Experts write to disk: keep each
  MoE layer's experts in the
  |docs-advanced_features-paged_experts-the-expert-cache|, so that later
  starts read them instead of loading and repacking them, and serve the
  experts that do not fit host memory from there (see
  |docs-advanced_features-paged_experts-disk-tier|). Off by default;
  requires `--enable-paged-experts`.
- `--paged-experts-host-memory-gb G`: Pinned host memory, in GiB, for the
  experts of all MoE layers. When every expert fits, nothing changes;
  otherwise the |docs-advanced_features-paged_experts-disk-tier| holds the
  rest, with `--paged-experts-enable-disk`, and without it the start fails.
  Unset, every expert is pinned as before; with
  `--paged-experts-enable-disk`, the experts that do not fit what is
  available at startup (within the container's memory limit) go to the disk
  tier, which then keeps 10 GiB of that free. Requires
  `--enable-paged-experts`.

*docs-advanced_features-paged_experts-supported-configurations-and-limitations*
SUPPORTED CONFIGURATIONS AND LIMITATIONS

- Quantization:

  Experts                           MoE runner  Notes
  --------------------------------  ----------  --------------------------------
  unquantized (bf16/fp16)           triton
  block-quantized FP8 (e.g.         triton
  weight_block_size [128, 128])
  compressed-tensors FP8,           triton      per-tensor FP8 is not supported
  per-channel or block, dynamic
  activations (e.g. FP8-dynamic
  checkpoints)
  W8A8 FP8 (--quantization          triton
  w8a8_fp8), W8A8 INT8
  (--quantization w8a8_int8)
  block-quantized INT8              triton
  GPTQ int4/int8, AWQ int4          Marlin
  compressed-tensors W4A16/W8A16    Marlin
  compressed-tensors NVFP4          Marlin      weight-only: nvfp4a16, or w4a4
                                                before Blackwell
  MXFP4 (e.g. gpt-oss)              Marlin      pass --moe-runner-backend marlin
  MXFP4 routed experts of an FP8    Marlin      pass --moe-runner-backend marlin
  checkpoint (e.g. DeepSeek-V4)
  ModelOpt NVFP4                    Marlin      pass --moe-runner-backend
                                                marlin; runs W4A16

  Other quantization methods and MoE runners are rejected at startup.
- Single GPU: tensor, expert, pipeline and data parallelism, EPLB, fused
  shared experts (use `--disable-shared-experts-fusion`) and
  `--enable-fused-moe-sum-all-reduce` are rejected at startup.
- Speculative decoding is rejected at startup.
- Load formats: `--load-format auto` (the default), `safetensors`, `pt`,
  `npcache`, `mistral`, `fastsafetensors`, `instanttensor` and
  `runai_streamer`. The others are rejected at startup: `dummy` has no real
  weights, `gguf` holds GGUF-quantized experts, and the rest load the
  weights without Paged Experts' loader and post-load step.
- CUDA graphs: decode graphs may use the `full` backend (the default) or be
  disabled; prefill graphs may use the `breakable` backend (the default on
  CUDA) or be disabled. Other combinations are rejected at startup.
- Host memory: the host store holds all E experts of every MoE layer and is
  page-locked, so the host must be able to pin that much memory, or the disk
  tier holds the rest. Under WSL2, pinned memory is capped at about half of
  system RAM: set `--paged-experts-host-memory-gb` below that.
- Disk tier (|docs-advanced_features-paged_experts-disk-tier|; R is the
  experts per layer in host memory): x86-64 hosts only for now. The first
  start writes every layer's file once, about the size of the expert
  weights, and keeps 8 GiB of the disk free; the space is checked at
  startup. The checkpoint must load through the safetensors loaders with
  mmap (see Startup; not a checkpoint that stacks all experts in one
  tensor), or the start fails. With decode CUDA graphs on and R < E, a step
  waits at a layer for the experts it reads from disk, and the scheduler
  thread waits for each decode step (no overlap scheduling); a step that
  gives up waiting (after 2 s) is replayed. On hybrid (mamba /
  linear-attention) models, the step's recurrent state is copied before it
  runs and restored before a replay. Refused then, as they accumulate state
  a replay would count twice: `--enable-linear-replayssm`,
  `--enable-linear-replayssm-spec`, `--enable-unified-memory`,
  `--expert-distribution-recorder-mode` and
  `SGLANG_OPT_USE_ONLINE_COMPRESS`. With `auto`, K grows at most to R.
- Startup: with mapped safetensors (`--load-format auto`, `safetensors` or
  `mistral`, without `--weight-loader-disable-mmap`), loading makes no
  second copy of the experts: each expert is read from the checkpoint once,
  straight into the pinned host store. With other loaders, and for
  checkpoints that store every expert in one tensor (e.g. gpt-oss), the
  experts are first loaded into a pageable copy of every expert, as large as
  the host store. With `--paged-experts-enable-disk`, later starts read the
  experts from the |docs-advanced_features-paged_experts-the-expert-cache|
  instead.

HOW IT WORKS               *docs-advanced_features-paged_experts-how-it-works*

    *docs-advanced_features-paged_experts-the-k-slot-table-and-the-host-store*
The K-slot table and the host store

The paged method wraps the layer's own fused-MoE method. It creates the
layer's expert tensors with K rows instead of E, so the GPU holds only the K
slots. Each tensor's weight loader is redirected: a load of one expert's
weights does not run yet, but waits as a view of the mapped checkpoint file.
After loading, the waiting loads run K experts at a time, each through
SGLang's native per-expert loader (sharding, gate/up placement, scale
layout) into K rows laid out as the GPU slots, and the wrapped method's
post-load step runs on those rows as it would without paging (on the Marlin
runner, the repack into Marlin's layout). Each chunk's result is copied into
the host store, a page-locked table of all E experts of each per-expert
tensor, and the chunk's checkpoint pages are given back to the kernel, so
the checkpoint never occupies memory beside the host store. The slots then
hold experts 0..K-1.

A repack must treat each expert on its own to run K at a time: the step runs
once more on experts 1..K in a chunk of their own and must give the same
bytes. A step that does not repack must leave the loaded weights as they
are, since paging copies host rows verbatim. Either is checked at startup.
Loads that cannot wait (a checkpoint tensor holding every expert, or a
loader whose tensors are not views of mapped files) go to a table of every
expert instead, which the chunks are taken from.

             *docs-advanced_features-paged_experts-a-step-waves-page-in-merge*
A step: waves, page-in, merge

Every forward step of every MoE layer:

1. The distinct experts the step routes to are split into waves of at most
   K, the experts already resident first. Decode at moderate batch sizes
   needs one wave; a prefill chunk usually needs several.
2. Each wave makes its experts resident, evicting the least recently used
   experts outside the wave, and copies the missing ones from the host store
   into their slots.
3. The routed expert ids are remapped to slots and the wrapped fused-MoE
   kernel runs over the wave's own entries without its final top-k sum,
   returning each routed (token, expert) output already multiplied by its
   router weight.
4. Each entry is written into one merged buffer by the one wave that holds
   its expert, and the merged entries go through the same top-k sum the
   kernel would have performed, so the result does not depend on how the
   experts were split into waves.

Captured decode         *docs-advanced_features-paged_experts-captured-decode*

With decode CUDA graphs on, a step whose routed entries fit the K slots
(`tokens × top_k ≤ K`, i.e. decode up to `K // top_k` requests) is served by
a single wave decided and paged on the GPU, with no host synchronization, so
the decode graph captures it:

- a JIT kernel makes the LRU decision on the device and writes the page-in
  plan (experts, slots, count) to GPU buffers;
- a second kernel copies the planned experts of every paged tensor from the
  pinned host store into their slots, reading the host memory directly
  through its unified address and the count on the device, so each graph
  replay moves exactly the experts it decided on;
- pre-copy: after a layer's copy, a side stream applies the next MoE layer's
  router to this layer's input and copies up to 3 of its predicted experts
  that are in none of its slots into its least recently used slots (never
  one holding a predicted expert), with a narrow grid beside this layer's
  compute; the next layer waits for it before it decides, so a right
  prediction takes a copy off the critical path. On for layers that route by
  plain softmax top-k (e.g. Qwen3-Next, Qwen3 MoE); others are skipped,
  logged at startup. It changes which experts are resident, not what is
  computed.

Decode capture batch sizes are capped at `K // top_k` (logged at startup);
larger batches run without a graph. Prefill steps plan their waves on the
host: under a breakable prefill graph the paged MoE layer is an eager break
between graph segments, so the rest of the layer stack stays captured. Both
paths share one LRU state, so residency carries over between captured and
uncaptured steps.

The expert cache       *docs-advanced_features-paged_experts-the-expert-cache*

Loading the experts takes most of a start for large MoE models, and formats
on the Marlin runner also repack them. With `--paged-experts-enable-disk`,
every MoE layer with more experts than K (under
`--paged-experts-num-resident auto`, more than the router's top-k: K is
sized after loading) keeps its experts on disk after loading, in the layout
of the host store, one file per layer under
`$SGLANG_CACHE_DIR/paged_experts/<model>-<key>/` (by default
`~/.cache/sglang`; `<model>` is the Hugging Face id, or the folder name and
a hash of its path). The files take about as much disk as the experts: on an
RTX 5070 Ti with 62 GB of RAM and a PCIe 5.0 NVMe, Qwen3-30B-A3B-GPTQ-Int4
keeps 13.9 GiB (`load_model` 33 s, 22 s from the cache), Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP8
27.0 GiB (51 s, 29 s) and Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct-NVFP4 40.7 GiB. After
loading, one log line names the model's directory and what the cache did:
layers read, rebuilt or written. Without the flag, a start whose experts the
cache could keep logs its size and location once.

- A later start reads the files instead of loading and repacking. It reads a
  layer's file straight into the host store, then still loads a few groups
  of experts from the checkpoint with the current code, each as wide as the
  router's top-k whatever K: the first experts, the last ones, the first
  ones shifted by one, and a group sampled anew at every start, so that over
  restarts every expert is checked. On the Marlin runner it repacks them. It
  compares their bytes with what it read; a file that does not give the same
  bytes for all of them, does not fit its layer or cannot be read is rebuilt
  from every expert and replaced, and a warning names the first group that
  differed. With mapped safetensors (see Startup), the other experts are not
  loaded at all unless the file is rebuilt; with other loaders, and for
  checkpoints that store every expert in one tensor, every expert is still
  loaded and the cache saves the repack only.
- The key covers the checkpoint files the loader read (path, size and
  modification time of the weight files and of the folder's `*.json`) and
  the torch, triton and kernel package versions (the model's directory), and
  per layer its format and MoE runner, its tensors and the content of the
  source files that repack the experts (the layer's file). A change to how
  the experts are loaded reaches every expert, so the checked groups catch
  it without a new key. The cache needs the default loader
  (`--load-format auto`, `safetensors`, `pt`, `npcache`, `mistral`,
  `fastsafetensors`, `instanttensor`), which reports the files it read.
- One set per model. Writing a file under a new key first removes the
  model's directories under other keys and the layer's file under another
  layer key, also to make the space for it. So the cache does not grow over
  time: it holds one set of files per model it has served. Starts that
  alternate `--quantization` or `--moe-runner-backend` on the same
  checkpoint replace each other's layer files at every start. Check the
  space with `du -sh $SGLANG_CACHE_DIR/paged_experts`; to clear a model,
  delete its `<model>-*` directory (the next start with the flag rebuilds
  it). A model loaded from a local folder gets a directory named by a hash;
  the startup log names it. An SGLang, torch or kernel package upgrade
  changes the key: the next start rebuilds every file once.
- Writes run in the background with direct I/O and are published complete or
  not at all (a staging file, then a rename), so concurrent starts can share
  the directory; a start that is killed mid-write leaves a staging file that
  a later start removes. A write is skipped when it would leave less than 8
  GiB free: on a nearly full disk, the layers written until then stay, and
  the warning says how much the next one needed. Reading or writing the
  cache never fails a start; it only costs the time it would have saved. On
  the |docs-advanced_features-paged_experts-disk-tier| the files are
  required instead: a first build that cannot write them fails the start.
- Who can write the directory controls the served weights: a start serves
  the cached experts outside the checked groups as they are on disk. Keep
  `$SGLANG_CACHE_DIR` private to the users who run the server, as for the
  other caches there.
- Not detected: a change that alters only some experts (for example a branch
  that depends on the values of their scales) outside the files in the key,
  until a sampled group covers one of those experts; and a checkpoint file
  or cache file altered in place, outside the checked groups, with its size
  and modification time kept (no checksum, as SGLang's other caches). If in
  doubt, delete the model's directory.

In a container, mount `$SGLANG_CACHE_DIR` (or a directory it points to) to
keep the files across restarts; without a mount they are written into the
container's own filesystem, which takes the disk space and loses them with
the container.

Disk tier                     *docs-advanced_features-paged_experts-disk-tier*

With `--paged-experts-enable-disk`, when the host budget cannot hold every
expert of every layer, each layer keeps all E experts in its
|docs-advanced_features-paged_experts-the-expert-cache| file and R of them
in pinned host rows; the K GPU slots are filled from the rows. The tier runs
on x86-64 hosts for now: on others (e.g. Grace), such a model fails at
startup. With `--paged-experts-host-memory-gb` and without
`--paged-experts-enable-disk`, such a model fails at startup with the sizes
and the flag. Layers routed by token id (DeepSeek-V4's hash layers) keep
every expert in host memory when they take at most half the budget; the
other layers split the rest evenly (over all hidden layers: a model with
dense layers pins less than the budget).

For example, DeepSeek-V4-Flash (137 GiB of experts) on a 16 GB GPU (RTX 5070
Ti) with 62 GB of RAM, as measured (about 14 tok/s decode; with the default
`--mem-fraction-static` the weights leave no room for the KV cache on this
card):

>sh
    SGLANG_OPT_FP8_WO_A_GEMM=1 python -m sglang.launch_server \
      --model-path deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 \
      --enable-paged-experts --paged-experts-enable-disk --paged-experts-host-memory-gb 45 \
      --moe-runner-backend marlin --mem-fraction-static 0.92 --max-running-requests 1 \
      --context-length 4096 --json-model-override-args '{"max_position_embeddings":4096}' \
      --chunked-prefill-size 4096 --swa-full-tokens-ratio 0.5 --cuda-graph-max-bs-decode 1 \
      --cuda-graph-backend-prefill disabled --disable-radix-cache
<
`SGLANG_OPT_FP8_WO_A_GEMM=1` keeps DeepSeek-V4's `wo_a` in FP8 on SM120
(upstream option), the 4096-token context limits the RoPE table and the KV
cache, and one prefill chunk per prompt reads each expert from disk once.

Set `--paged-experts-host-memory-gb` on a machine where the rest of the
server needs more than 10 GiB of host memory: pinned memory cannot be
swapped out.

DeepSeek-V4 on a small GPU needs `--max-running-requests`: without it,
SGLang reserves the per-request state of DeepSeek-V4's compressed attention
for its default of 256 requests (about 2.5 GB for DeepSeek-V4-Flash) before
Paged Experts sizes anything, which can leave no room for the sliding-window
pool and fail the start. `--max-running-requests 1` reserves it for one.

- The first start writes the files once, so a model larger than RAM never
  has to fit in RAM: the experts' loads are replayed K at a time from the
  mapped checkpoint (see Startup) straight into the file being built (a
  write through a mapping of the file, not direct I/O), through the repack
  on the Marlin runner. The build keeps 8 GiB of the disk free: its space is
  checked at startup, and again for each file. A failed build leaves no file
  behind. Later starts check the same experts as for a model that fits and
  do not read the other experts from the checkpoint; nor do they read them
  from the file, except the ones the slots and host rows start with.
- The host rows are inclusive: moving an expert into a slot copies it from
  its host row, which keeps it; the expert the slot held is dropped (the
  disk has it), so nothing is written back. An expert only on disk is first
  read into the least recently used host row (whose expert is dropped), with
  one read per expert, bypassing the page cache (`O_DIRECT`), and several in
  flight.
- Captured decode decides on the GPU as before and copies the experts that
  are in host rows inside the graph. An expert only on disk is flagged: the
  layer's plan kernel writes the layer's state to pinned host memory before
  the layer copies its host-row hits, a host thread reads the flagged
  experts while those copies run, and the step waits at the layer until they
  are in their slots, then runs on with the experts it routed to. The host
  thread is the one that replays the graph, so it returns once the step
  ends: the overlap scheduler cannot prepare the next batch during a decode
  step. A step that gives up waiting (after 2 s) runs on, and the host
  copies the experts in after it and replays the step, with the recurrent
  state restored; the log warns about such steps. A decode step only writes
  its own KV entries and outputs, so replaying it gives the same result.
  ReplaySSM, `--enable-unified-memory`,
  `--expert-distribution-recorder-mode` and DeepSeek-V4's
  `SGLANG_OPT_USE_ONLINE_COMPRESS` accumulate state a replay would count
  twice: they are refused with decode CUDA graphs.
- Prefill reads from disk: a prompt of a few thousand tokens routes to
  nearly every expert of every layer, so its time to first token is that of
  reading most of the experts (DeepSeek-V4-Flash: about 8.5 s for a
  1.5k-token prompt on a PCIe 5.0 NVMe).
- Checkpoints: the tier needs the experts' loads as views of mapped
  safetensors files, one tensor per expert (`--load-format auto`,
  `safetensors` or `mistral`): checkpoints that stack all experts in one
  tensor (gpt-oss) are refused.

Expert packs (`--load-format expert_pack`) are a different SSD tier:
prebuilt packs for specific models, read from SSD into a GPU cache. The disk
tier needs no preparation; it serves checkpoints that load as mapped
safetensors with one tensor per expert.

CHOOSING K                   *docs-advanced_features-paged_experts-choosing-k*

The K-slot table and the KV cache come out of the same static budget
(`--mem-fraction-static`). One resident expert per layer costs
`per_expert_bytes × num_moe_layers` of GPU memory; the more experts stay
resident, the fewer are paged in per step and the faster decode is, up to a
plateau.

`auto` (the default)   *docs-advanced_features-paged_experts-auto-the-default*

With `--paged-experts-num-resident auto`, or the flag omitted, K is chosen
once every weight is loaded, in two steps:

1. The KV cache comes first. By default it keeps room for one request of the
   model's own context. `--context-length` sets that length, and
   `--max-running-requests`, if you set it, how many such requests it aims
   to hold at once: one full-length request is a promise, more of them a
   target that the experts never take memory from. `--max-total-tokens` sets
   the KV cache's size directly instead. As always in SGLang, requests
   beyond what the KV cache holds at a time queue.
2. The experts take the rest. What the static budget has left after the KV
   cache is allocated goes to the expert slots, one slot per layer at a
   time, up to all experts.

So under `auto`, `--context-length`, `--max-running-requests` and
`--max-total-tokens` decide the KV cache, and they are also the knobs that
trade context and concurrency for resident experts. At startup the server
logs the chosen K, the KV cache it kept and why, and how many full-length
requests fit at once:

>text
    Paged experts: K=63 of 128 experts per MoE layer resident (6.85 GiB); KV cache 40960 tokens,
    1 request(s) of 40960 at once (aim 40960: the model's context 40960 x 1 request(s)). To pin:
    --paged-experts-num-resident 63
<
If a `--max-total-tokens` you set, or one request of a `--context-length`
you set, cannot be met even at K = `top_k`, the server stops at startup and
names the flag. If fewer requests of that length fit than
`--max-running-requests` asks for, the log says how many do, and the rest
queue. If one request of the model's own context does not fit, K stays at
`top_k`, the KV cache takes what is left, and requests are capped at its
size, as SGLang caps them whenever the KV cache is shorter than the context;
a warning says so.

On hybrid models with Mamba layers and no `--max-mamba-cache-size`, the
Mamba state pool holds the requests the KV cache aims for: the
`--max-running-requests` you set, or one; never more than SGLang's own share
of the budget (`--mamba-full-memory-ratio`), and never so many that one
full-length request no longer fits in the KV cache next to it: the rest
queue. Each running request needs its own Mamba state however short it is,
so these are the requests that run at a time: without
`--max-running-requests`, one. SGLang's startup warning that requests are
capped by the Mamba state refers to this; set `--max-running-requests` to
run more.

Ways to give the experts more memory:

- a shorter `--context-length` or `--max-total-tokens`, if your requests are
  shorter than the model's context, or fewer `--max-running-requests`;
- `--kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3`, which halves the KV cache's cost per token;
- a larger `--mem-fraction-static`, if the GPU has activation memory to
  spare.

`auto` cannot be combined with `--enable-memory-saver`, `--enable-lora`,
`--enable-nvidia-megakernel` or post-capture KV sizing
(`SGLANG_ENABLE_POST_CAPTURE_KV_SIZING`); set an explicit K with those.

An explicit K             *docs-advanced_features-paged_experts-an-explicit-k*

`--paged-experts-num-resident K` is used as given, and the KV cache takes
what is left, as without paging; if the server then runs out of memory for
the KV cache at startup, lower K. The K that `auto` logs can be pinned this
way.

For example, Qwen3-30B-A3B-GPTQ-Int4 (2.43 MB per expert, 48 MoE layers, 117
MB per slot) on a 16 GB GPU with `--mem-fraction-static 0.88` (the log
above): its own 40,960-token context leaves K = 63 of 128 experts (208
tok/s), `--context-length 16384` K = 86 (231 tok/s) and
`--max-total-tokens 10240` K = 92 (233 tok/s). Decode speed on this model is
flat from K ≈ 88 up and falls below it.

CORRECTNESS                 *docs-advanced_features-paged_experts-correctness*

Prompt and greedy decode logprobs are compared with the unpaged server under
`--enable-deterministic-inference --attention-backend triton`, eager and
with decode captured:

- triton runner (unquantized, FP8, INT8): bit-identical;
- Marlin runner (GPTQ, AWQ, compressed-tensors, MXFP4, NVFP4): Marlin's
  reduction depends on the batch shape, so a paged step (which runs the
  kernel on a different number of experts) differs from the unpaged one
  within Marlin's own batch-to-batch noise. On SM90 and newer the Marlin MoE
  kernel also reduces with atomic adds and is not reproducible from run to
  run (two identical unpaged NVFP4 servers differ by up to about 1 nat).
  Accuracy is unchanged: on GSM8K (200 questions), gpt-oss-20b MXFP4 scores
  0.96--0.97 paged (16 of 32 experts resident) and 0.975 unpaged.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------
PD Disaggregation            *sglang-docs-advanced_features-pd_disaggregation*

  *docs-advanced_features-pd_disaggregation-why-and-what-is-pd-disaggregation*
WHY AND WHAT IS PD DISAGGREGATION?

Large Language Model (LLM) inference comprises two distinct phases: Prefill
and Decode. The Prefill phase is computation-intensive, processing the
entire input sequence, while the Decode phase is memory-intensive, managing
the Key-Value (KV) cache for token generation. Traditionally, these phases
are handled within a unified engine, where combined scheduling of prefill
and decode batches introduces inefficiencies. To address these challenges,
we introduce Prefill and Decoding (PD) Disaggregation in SGLang.

     *docs-advanced_features-pd_disaggregation-issues-with-unified-scheduling*
Issues with Unified Scheduling

The conventional unified engine, which processes prefill and decode batches
together, results in two significant problems:

1. Prefill Interruption: Incoming prefill batches frequently interrupt
   ongoing decode batches, causing substantial delays in token generation.
2. DP Attention Imbalance: In data-parallel (DP) attention, one DP worker
   may process a prefill batch while another handles a decode batch
   simultaneously, leading to increased decode latency.

PD Disaggregation resolves these by separating the two stages, enabling
tailored optimizations for each.

For the design details, please refer to link
https://docs.google.com/document/d/1rQXJwKd5b9b1aOzLh98mnyMhBMhlxXA5ATZTHoQrwvc/edit?tab=t.0.

Currently, we support Mooncake and NIXL as the transfer engine.

           *docs-advanced_features-pd_disaggregation-decode-allocation-policy*
DECODE ALLOCATION POLICY

By default, decode reserves each request's destination KV slots before
prefill finishes. Long prefills can hold these slots while decode waits for
the KV data. To delay this reservation, set the following flag on both
prefill and decode:

>sh
    --disaggregation-decode-allocation-policy prefill_complete
<
With `prefill_complete`, prefill computes without waiting for destination
slots, then signals readiness after accepting its final prefill result.
Decode reserves slots and starts the existing KV transfer handshake only
after that signal. This changes per-request KV reservation, not the size or
creation of the global KV pool. The default `early` policy preserves the
existing behavior.

Deferring allocation can help when long prefills compete with active decode
requests for destination KV capacity. It also retains KV on prefill longer
and removes overlap between chunked prefill and KV transfer. Compare both
policies for your workload; this option is not a general throughput
improvement.

This initial implementation requires Mooncake (RDMA or `mooncake_tcp`), the
Python bootstrap registry, and attention TP/CP and pipeline sizes of one.
Attention DP is allowed when each DP rank has attention TP size one. Prefill
automatically resolves `--optimistic-prefill-attempts` from zero to one;
configurations that disable optimistic prefill after model validation are
rejected. Chunked prefill does not yield just because decode has not
admitted the request. Completed requests retain their KV in the existing
optimistic-prefill inflight queue until decode supplies destination indices;
readiness alone never starts a KV write. After a successful transfer,
prefill clears the room's readiness and transfer state before notifying
decode of success. Retraction recovery can then reuse the same bootstrap
room. This notification waits for worker and scheduler cleanup; failure and
cancellation records remain until their timeout expires. Retries remain
eligible for prefill after the optimistic attempt budget is exhausted and
remain subject to the existing cancellation and timeout handling.

On prefill, `SGLANG_DISAGGREGATION_BOOTSTRAP_TIMEOUT` starts after the final
prefill result, giving decode admission its own budget. On decode,
`SGLANG_DISAGGREGATION_WAITING_TIMEOUT` bounds the wait for prefill
completion, then starts afresh for admission and again when destination
indices are sent for transfer.

The option does not support staging buffers, runtime PD role switching,
encoder disaggregation, decoupled speculation, HiSparse, decode radix cache,
decode HiCache, or non-DSA auxiliary state pools. Prefill HiCache is limited
to L2 with `write_back` and no storage backend. Unsupported configurations
fail validation.

All communicating workers must use the same revision and enable the same
policy. This version of the decode worker rejects policy or peer-layout
mismatches before destination registration. Older decode workers do not
enforce this check. Keep `early` on both sides until every worker has been
upgraded, then enable the new policy on both sides.

*docs-advanced_features-pd_disaggregation-profiling-in-pd-disaggregation-mode*
PROFILING IN PD DISAGGREGATION MODE

When you need to profile prefill or decode workers in PD disaggregation
mode, please refer to the Profile In PD Disaggregation Mode
https://docs.sglang.io/docs/developer_guide/benchmark_and_profiling#profile-in-pd-disaggregation-mode
section in the Benchmark and Profiling guide. Due to torch profiler
limitations, prefill and decode workers must be profiled separately using
dedicated command-line options.

                 *docs-advanced_features-pd_disaggregation-router-integration*
ROUTER INTEGRATION

For deploying PD disaggregation at scale with load balancing and fault
tolerance, SGLang provides a router. The router can distribute requests
between prefill and decode instances using various routing policies.

The router is the `sgl-router` binary. It is pre-installed on the `PATH` of
the SGLang Docker images; otherwise install it with
`pip install sgl-router`, or see
|docs-advanced_features-dp_dpa_router_guide-quick-start-for-sgl-router| for
the container image and building from source.

Launch it in front of the prefill and decode servers:

[Command]

[Command]Command

>sh
    sgl-router \
      --model-id meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct \
      --no-tokenizer \
      --worker-urls http://127.0.0.1:30000 http://127.0.0.1:30001 \
      --host 0.0.0.0 \
      --port 8000
<
`--worker-urls` lists the prefill and decode servers together: the router
reads each server's role and the prefill bootstrap port from the server
itself. `--model-id` must match the servers' model name, which is their
`--served-model-name`, or their `--model-path` when that flag is not set.
`--no-tokenizer` leaves tokenization to the servers. Wait for
`curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/readiness` to return HTTP 200, which means both
servers are registered. For routing policies, Kubernetes service discovery,
and the other flags, see `sgl-router --help` and the sgl-router README
https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/sgl-router/README.md.

        *docs-advanced_features-pd_disaggregation-responses-api-under-http-pd*
Responses API under HTTP PD

HTTP PD supports foreground generation through `POST /v1/responses`,
including streaming generation with `stream=true` through the HTTP PD
router. This requires both the router's Responses dispatch support and
serving workers that accept Responses PD routing metadata.

Store-backed and stateful Responses features are not supported under PD:

- Response persistence (`store`) and response history.
- Conversation chaining with `previous_response_id`.
- Background Responses (`background=true`), including background streams.
- Retrieval by response ID (`GET /v1/responses/{id}`).
- Cancel-by-ID (`POST /v1/responses/{id}/cancel`).
- Other workflows requiring shared process-local Responses history.

Prefill and decode run in separate serving processes. Their process-local
Responses stores cannot provide coherent shared state: both legs need the
same conversation history to reconstruct the prompt, and prefill's stored
response is not available to decode. Send explicit conversation history in
foreground requests instead of relying on stored response IDs.

Built-in tools (`web_search`, `code_interpreter`) are also unsupported under
PD: each tool call requires another generation, but the router dispatches
exactly one prefill/decode pair per HTTP request.

Serving-side capability enforcement is tracked in #39122
https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/39122. That change introduces
opt-in standalone storage with `--enable-response-store`, disallows it under
PD, and rejects stateful requests with HTTP 400 before generation. These
checks require a serving version containing that change; older versions must
not be assumed to reject every unsupported workflow at admission. The HTTP
PD router also rejects detached background requests because it does not
implement their retrieval/cancel lifecycle.

MOONCAKE                   *docs-advanced_features-pd_disaggregation-mooncake*

Requirements           *docs-advanced_features-pd_disaggregation-requirements*

>sh
    uv pip install mooncake-transfer-engine
<
On Intel XPU, the PyPI wheel has no XPU support. Use the XPU Docker image
(`docker/xpu.Dockerfile`), or build Mooncake from source with icpx and
`-DUSE_XPU=ON -DUSE_TENT=ON`; see Intel GPUs (XPU)
https://docs.sglang.io/docs/hardware-platforms/xpu for the runtime settings.

AWS EFA                     *docs-advanced_features-pd_disaggregation-aws-efa*

           *docs-advanced_features-pd_disaggregation-efa-in-the-docker-images*
EFA in the Docker images

All CUDA 13 images include the AWS EFA userspace (libfabric with the EFA
provider, the aws-ofi-nccl plugin, and hwloc) and a Mooncake build with the
EFA transport, so the host does not need its own EFA userspace install. The
host still needs the EFA kernel driver.

To use EFA, pass the EFA devices into the container, lift the locked-memory
limit, and set:

- `MOONCAKE_PROTOCOL=efa`, so Mooncake uses EFA.
- `SGLANG_DISAGGREGATION_NIXL_BACKEND=LIBFABRIC`, so NIXL transfers use EFA.
- `NCCL_NET_PLUGIN=ofi` and `NCCL_TUNER_PLUGIN=ofi`, so NCCL uses
  aws-ofi-nccl.

>sh
    HF_CACHE_DIR="/path/to/huggingface-cache"
    docker run -it --gpus all \
      --network host \
      --ipc=host \
      $(for d in /dev/infiniband/uverbs*; do echo -n "--device $d "; done) \
      --ulimit memlock=-1 \
      -v "$HF_CACHE_DIR:/root/.cache/huggingface" \
      --env HF_TOKEN \
      --env MOONCAKE_PROTOCOL=efa \
      --env SGLANG_DISAGGREGATION_NIXL_BACKEND=LIBFABRIC \
      --env NCCL_NET_PLUGIN=ofi \
      --env NCCL_TUNER_PLUGIN=ofi \
      lmsysorg/sglang:latest bash
<
Inside the container, `fi_info -p efa -t FI_EP_RDM` lists the EFA devices.

  *docs-advanced_features-pd_disaggregation-install-into-your-own-environment*
Install into your own environment

`mooncake-transfer-engine-cuda13` 0.3.14 and later include the EFA transport
on x86_64 and aarch64, so no separate EFA package is needed. If an
environment still has `mooncake-transfer-engine-efa-cuda13`, uninstall it
first: both packages install the same `mooncake` Python module.

>sh
    python3 -m pip uninstall -y mooncake-transfer-engine-efa-cuda13
    python3 -m pip install --no-deps "mooncake-transfer-engine-cuda13>=0.3.14"

    export LD_LIBRARY_PATH="/opt/amazon/efa/lib:/opt/amazon/efa/lib64:${LD_LIBRARY_PATH:-}"
    export MOONCAKE_PROTOCOL=efa

    python3 -c 'from mooncake import engine; assert engine.SUPPORT_EFA'
    fi_info -p efa -t FI_EP_RDM
<
The Mooncake wheel does not bundle `libfabric` or `libefa`, so the host
needs a compatible AWS EFA userspace installation.

               *docs-advanced_features-pd_disaggregation-cuda-vmm-limitations*
CUDA VMM limitations

These limitations apply whenever `MOONCAKE_PROTOCOL=efa`, including in the
EFA Docker images.

The current libfabric EFA provider cannot transfer CUDA VMM-backed buffers.
Until libfabric issue #12853 https://github.com/ofiwg/libfabric/issues/12853
is resolved, apply these settings to both prefill and decode workers:

- Do not set `SGLANG_MOONCAKE_CUSTOM_MEM_POOL` to `NVLINK` or `BAREX`.
  `INTRA_NODE_NVLINK` is supported because it uses the default CUDA
  allocator.
- Do not enable `expandable_segments:True` in `PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF` or
  `PYTORCH_ALLOC_CONF`.
- Post-capture KV sizing is automatically disabled for the EFA protocol
  because its KV cache uses CUDA VMM allocations.
- Do not set `MC_FORCE_MNNVL` or `NCCL_MNNVL_ENABLE`; EFA is not an MNNVL
  transport.

SGLang validates the first two constraints at startup to avoid a later
`fi_read` or `fi_write` failure from libfabric.

            *docs-advanced_features-pd_disaggregation-ib-device-configuration*
IB Device Configuration

`--disaggregation-ib-device` supports the following formats when using the
Mooncake backend:

1. Shared device list for all GPUs: `mlx5_0` or `mlx5_0,mlx5_1`
2. Per-GPU JSON mapping: `{"0": "mlx5_0,mlx5_1", "1": "mlx5_2,mlx5_3"}`
3. Path to a JSON file containing the same per-GPU mapping

Each JSON value uses the same comma-separated device list format as the
shared configuration.

     *docs-advanced_features-pd_disaggregation-nvlink-transport-configuration*
NVLink Transport Configuration

To enable NVLink transport for KV cache transfers with the mooncake backend
(recommended for NVL72 deployments), set the following environment
variables. Note that auxiliary data transfer will still use TCP as a
temporary workaround.

[Command]

[Command]Command

>sh
    export SGLANG_MOONCAKE_CUSTOM_MEM_POOL=NVLINK
    export MC_FORCE_MNNVL=True
<
To utilize Intra-Node NVLink for KV cache transfers with the Mooncake
backend (recommended for A100, H20, H100, etc.), set the following
environment variables. Please note that auxiliary data still needs to be
transferred via TCP.

>sh
    export SGLANG_MOONCAKE_CUSTOM_MEM_POOL=INTRA_NODE_NVLINK
    export MC_INTRANODE_NVLINK=true
<
The `SGLANG_MOONCAKE_CUSTOM_MEM_POOL` environment variable enables the
custom memory pool. Supported values are `NVLINK` (or `True`), `BAREX`, and
`INTRA_NODE_NVLINK`. These pools use Mooncake's CUDA allocators and are
CUDA-only; do not set them on Intel XPU.

*docs-advanced_features-pd_disaggregation-heterogeneous-tp-with-gpu-staging-buffer*
HETEROGENEOUS TP WITH GPU STAGING BUFFER

When prefill and decode use different tensor parallelism (TP) sizes (e.g.,
prefill TP=4, decode DP attention with TP=1), the KV cache memory layout
differs between the two sides. The GPU staging buffer solves this by
gathering KV head slices into a contiguous buffer on the prefill side,
performing bulk RDMA transfer, then scattering into the correct KV cache
pages on the decode side. This provides 2--5x throughput improvement over
the default per-token slice approach at high concurrency and matches
homogeneous TP baselines within ~5%.

Enable the staging buffer when prefill and decode use different TP sizes
with the Mooncake transfer backend. When both sides use the same TP size,
staging is automatically bypassed even if enabled.

  Note: The staging buffer is designed for non-MLA models (e.g. GQA, MHA).
  MLA models (e.g. DeepSeek-V2/V3) should not enable this flag.

  Note: The staging buffer also runs on Intel XPU, tested with prefill TP 1
  and decode TP 2 on the Mooncake backend. On XPU, Mooncake needs a build
  with `-DUSE_XPU=ON -DUSE_TENT=ON` and runs with `MC_USE_TENT=1`.

  Note: You can use different attention TP sizes for hybrid sliding-window
  models (e.g. `openai/gpt-oss-120b`) with Mooncake or NIXL. For unequal TP,
  both backends transfer the sliding-window KV by token and KV-head slice.
  The staging buffer carries only full-attention KV. Use `--pp-size 1` and
  leave `--enable-unified-memory` disabled for this configuration. MXFP8 KV
  cache is not supported for unequal-TP SWA transfer.

              *docs-advanced_features-pd_disaggregation-environment-variables*
Environment Variables

Variable                            Description                        Default
----------------------------------  ---------------------------------  -------
SGLANG_DISAGG_STAGING_BUFFER        Enable GPU staging buffer for      False
                                    heterogeneous TP KV transfer
SGLANG_DISAGG_STAGING_POOL_SIZE_MB  Decode-side ring buffer pool       4096
                                    total size in MB

Usage Example         *docs-advanced_features-pd_disaggregation-usage-example*

[Command]

[Command]Command

>sh
    # Set staging buffer environment variables on BOTH prefill and decode
    export SGLANG_DISAGG_STAGING_BUFFER=1
    export SGLANG_DISAGG_STAGING_POOL_SIZE_MB=4096

    # Prefill with TP=4
    python -m sglang.launch_server \
      --model-path $MODEL_PATH \
      --disaggregation-mode prefill \
      --port 30000 \
      --tp 4 \
      --trust-remote-code \
      --disaggregation-ib-device mlx5_1,mlx5_2

    # Decode with TP=1 (or DP attention with effective attention TP=1)
    python -m sglang.launch_server \
      --model-path $MODEL_PATH \
      --disaggregation-mode decode \
      --port 30001 \
      --tp 4 \
      --attn-dp-size 4 \
      --trust-remote-code \
      --disaggregation-ib-device mlx5_3,mlx5_4

    # Router
    sgl-router \
      --model-id $MODEL_PATH \
      --no-tokenizer \
      --worker-urls http://127.0.0.1:30000 http://127.0.0.1:30001 \
      --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000

Advanced Configuration

             *docs-advanced_features-pd_disaggregation-nixl-backend-selection*
NIXL Backend Selection

By default, NIXL uses the UCX backend for KV cache transfers. You can select
a different NIXL plugin backend depending on your infrastructure using the
environment variable `SGLANG_DISAGGREGATION_NIXL_BACKEND`.

Example: `export SGLANG_DISAGGREGATION_NIXL_BACKEND=LIBFABRIC`

Available backends: UCX (default), LIBFABRIC, or any installed NIXL plugin.

Example usage:

>sh
    export SGLANG_DISAGGREGATION_NIXL_BACKEND=LIBFABRIC
    python -m sglang.launch_server \
      --model-path meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct \
      --disaggregation-mode prefill \
      --disaggregation-transfer-backend nixl \
      --port 30000
<

               *docs-advanced_features-pd_disaggregation-ucx-device-selection*
UCX device selection

For NVIDIA CUDA and AMD ROCm deployments using NIXL UCX,
`--disaggregation-ib-device` accepts a shared HCA list or a per-GPU
JSON/file mapping. Mapping keys are process-visible GPU IDs; use HCA names
without port suffixes, such as `mlx5_0`.

A non-empty `UCX_NET_DEVICES` takes precedence over this CLI option. SGLang
leaves the environment variable unchanged and skips the CLI mapping,
including per-GPU mappings, with a warning. This preserves interfaces such
as `lo` in an existing configuration like `rdma0:1,rdma4:1,lo`, which some
RoCE hosts need for NIXL's self-endpoint.

To use per-GPU CLI selection, unset `UCX_NET_DEVICES`; keep it configured on
hosts that require the loopback entry. An explicit `device_list` in
`SGLANG_DISAGGREGATION_NIXL_BACKEND_PARAMS` is left unchanged and still
overrides `UCX_NET_DEVICES`; do not set it if you rely on the environment's
complete device list.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------
                          *sglang-docs-advanced_features-pipeline_parallelism*
Pipeline Parallelism for Long Context

        *docs-advanced_features-pipeline_parallelism-why-pipeline-parallelism*
WHY PIPELINE PARALLELISM?

As Large Language Models (LLMs) scale toward trillion-parameter
architectures and “infinite” context windows, the underlying serving
infrastructure must evolve toward more granular, cross-node parallelization
strategies. While KV cache techniques effectively mitigate redundant
computation, they cannot circumvent the prohibitive Time to First Token
(TTFT) inherent in ultra-long sequences with extremely large initial Input
Token Length (ITL). Although Tensor Parallelism (TP) remains the
conventional approach for intra-node scaling, it frequently encounters
communication bottlenecks during multi-node deployments. On the other hand,
pipeline parallelism only requires cross-node communication at the
boundaries of each pipeline stage, which can achieve better
computation-communication overlap compared to a large TP. Therefore, it is
also a promising parallelization strategy for improving throughput.

Detailed analysis can be found in this blog
https://lmsys.org/blog/2026-01-15-chunked-pipeline/.

*docs-advanced_features-pipeline_parallelism-implementation-refactoring-based-on-async-communication*
IMPLEMENTATION REFACTORING BASED ON ASYNC COMMUNICATION

With Dynamic Chunked Prefill, pipeline parallelism has the potential to
reduce the TTFT of long-context inputs. For each request, its input tokens
can be partitioned into multiple chunks, each no longer than the chunked
prefill size. Different chunks of the same request can be processed
simultaneously by different nodes, thus parallelizing the processing and
reducing TTFT. SGLang has supported Pipeline Parallelism (#5724) for some
time and made it compatible with the PD Disaggregation feature (#8846), but
the implementation was not perfect and had significant room for performance
improvements.

To eliminate this performance hazard, SGLang implements a Micro-batching
Event Loop with non-blocking asynchronous peer-to-peer (P2P) communication
to overlap GPU computation with CPU metadata processing and PP
communication. This ensures that while one micro-batch is being computed on
the GPU, the next one is already being prepared and moved into position
effectively, ensuring the pipeline remains as saturated as possible. This
approach was first proposed in #7979 and has been redesigned and included in
#11852.

The key mechanisms of the implementation include:

- Decoupled Sync/Async Logic in the Event Loop: The scheduler uses
  `async_send` in `_pp_send_pyobj_to_next_stage`. Instead of waiting for a
  transfer to complete, it returns a `P2PWork` handle. The actual
  synchronization (`P2PWork.work.wait()`) is deferred until
  `_pp_commit_comm_work` is called, allowing the CPU to perform other
  work---like scheduling the next batch or processing metadata---while data
  is in flight.
- Multi-Stream Execution: In addition to the main `default_stream`, which
  serves as the synchronization stream, SGLang utilizes dedicated
  `forward_stream` and `copy_stream` to execute forward pass GPU computation
  and Data-to-Host (D2H) memory transfers separately for better overlapping.
  While `_pp_launch_batch` is executing the current micro-batch on the GPU
  for the current stage, the CPU processes the previous micro-batch's
  results using `_pp_process_batch_result`.

 *docs-advanced_features-pipeline_parallelism-guidance-about-dynamic-chunking*
GUIDANCE ABOUT DYNAMIC CHUNKING

            *docs-advanced_features-pipeline_parallelism-why-dynamic-chunking*
Why Dynamic Chunking

Chunked prefill with a fixed size can cause bubbles in the pipeline,
especially when the pp size is large. The main reason behind this phenomenon
is that the model has a non-uniform running time, even though each chunk
size is identical (brought by the Transformer structure). The larger the
prefix sequence length, the longer the running time of the chunk. And these
bubbles will be propagated to the next stage, and will significantly degrade
the scale efficiency of larger pp ranks.

To address this issue, SGLang introduces a dynamic chunking mechanism to
predict the optimal size for the next chunk such that it satisfies this
condition:

Runtime(L + Next Chunk Size) - Runtime(L) = Runtime(Initial Chunk Size)

where L denotes the Prefix Sequence Length. By profiling a series of
requests with different ITLs, we model the cumulative runtime as a quadratic
function of sequence length. Using this model, we solve the optimal next
chunk size for any given prefix length L. Since the computation complexity
of the Attention mechanism scales with L, the next chunk size will be
progressively reduced as L grows to maintain an aligned chunk execution time
across pipeline stages.

Based on this method, the scheduler can predict and dynamically reduce the
chunk size during runtime to minimize the bubbles caused by the stage
misalignment. To be noticed, the scheduler does not use the raw predicted
value. To facilitate efficient KVCache memory management and ensure affinity
with hardware execution efficiency, the value is aligned downward to the
nearest multiple of max(`--page-size`, 64).

*docs-advanced_features-pipeline_parallelism-chunked-prefill-size-and-smoothing-factor*
Chunked Prefill Size and Smoothing Factor

When `--enable-dynamic-chunking` is enabled, each chunk size of a sequence
is determined dynamically based on the quadratic model that predicts the
next chunk size based on the estimated runtime of the initial chunk length.
In this case, we use `--chunked-prefill-size` to set up the initial chunk
size. When switching to the dynamic chunking mode, the initial chunk size
(`--chunked-prefill-size`) should be set to a larger value comparable to the
original chunked prefill size, so that there won't be too many chunks.

`SGLANG_DYNAMIC_CHUNKING_SMOOTH_FACTOR` is an environmental variable that
controls the smoothing factor for the dynamic chunking algorithm, defaulting
to 0.75. It determines how much the chunk size can change during the prefill
phase. A larger value means a more aggressive chunk size change, which may
lead to better performance but also to greater chunk size changes (the chunk
size at the end may become very small, which could lead to performance
degradation) and more total chunks. When it is set to 1, the chunk size will
be adjusted strictly based on the aforementioned quadratic model that
predicts the next chunk size. A smaller value means a more conservative
chunk size change, which may lead to smaller chunk size changes and fewer
total chunks. When it is set to 0, the chunk size will not be adjusted
dynamically, so it is identical to the traditional way with a fixed chunked
prefill size.

Due to the variation in hardware, models, and target workloads, a static
configuration is seldom optimal across all scenarios. Consequently,
achieving peak performance necessitates a degree of hyperparameter tuning
when switching to the dynamic chunking mode.

Tuning Guidance for Dynamic Chunked Prefill

- Step 1 - Iterate to find the optimal fixed chunked prefill size for the
  targeted PP size: Different PP sizes for targeted ITL may have different
  optimal chunked prefill sizes. Therefore, users should iterate to obtain
  the baseline according to the available resources for scaling.
- Step 2 - Initial Chunk Size Selection for Dynamic Chunking: Set the
  initial size to 2× or 3× the optimal fixed chunked prefill size. This
  reduces the total number of chunks and prevents “tail chunks” from
  underutilizing hardware. To maintain efficiency for extremely large Input
  Token Lengths (ITL), the dynamic predictor automatically ensures
  subsequent chunks are at least 1/4 of this initial size. In addition, it
  is recommended to use a larger initial chunk size (e.g., 4× the optimal
  fixed chunked prefill size) for such cases as well.
- Step 3 - Smooth Factor Adjustment: This factor controls how strictly the
  chunk size adjusts the prediction given by the quadratic performance
  fitting model.
  - 1.0: Follows the model strictly.
  - 0.6 -- 0.85 (Recommended): Typical range for the best balance between
    dynamic scaling and hardware stability. Through experiments, we find
    that a range between 0.6 and 0.85 typically yields the best performance
    for dynamic chunking.
  - 0: Disables dynamic adjustment, reverting to traditional fixed-size
    chunking.
- Another small optimization tip: Put the larger partition in the higher PP
  rank when the layers are not evenly divisible across ranks. It can
  increase the GPU utilization when a larger PP rank is waiting for the
  previous stage's result, hence reducing the bubbles on higher PP ranks. If
  we take DeepSeek-V3.1 as an example,
  `SGLANG_PP_LAYER_PARTITION=15,15,15,16` usually performs better than
  `16,15,15,15`.

  *docs-advanced_features-pipeline_parallelism-best-practice-for-long-context*
BEST PRACTICE FOR LONG CONTEXT

 *docs-advanced_features-pipeline_parallelism-tuning-the-chunked-prefill-size*
Tuning the Chunked Prefill Size

Optimizing the chunked prefill size is crucial for balancing pipeline
efficiency and resource utilization. The ideal size depends on factors
including model architecture, hardware configuration, and typical input
lengths. We recommend starting with a small chunk size, such as 4K, and
gradually increasing it until you find the optimal size for your specific
use case (Different targeted ITL and PP Sizes may have different optimal
chunked prefill sizes. Therefore, users should iterate to obtain the
baseline according to the available resources for scaling). Alternatively,
you can analyze the hardware capacity and determine the optimal chunk size
based on the roofline model.

*docs-advanced_features-pipeline_parallelism-enable-dynamic-chunking-and-adjust-smoothing-factor-for-ultra-long-itl*
Enable Dynamic Chunking and Adjust Smoothing Factor for Ultra-long ITL

SGLang also offers a dynamic chunking solution that could further improve
performance. This feature is currently an experimental feature that requires
a certain amount of tuning experimentation and may not be suitable for all
workloads. In addition, fine-tuning the smoothing factor can help optimize
performance for specific workloads and model characteristics.

        *docs-advanced_features-pipeline_parallelism-case-study-on-nvidia-h20*
Case Study on NVIDIA H20

When evaluating pipeline parallelism with fixed chunked prefill sizes from
2K to 16K, experiment results show that a 4K chunk size delivered optimal
prefill TTFT performance for the DeepSeek-V3.1, and a 6K chunk size
delivered optimal prefill TTFT performance for the Qwen3-235B-A22B-FP8.

When enabling dynamic chunking, we first scale the optimal fixed chunked
prefill size by a factor of 3 as the initial chunk size. Through
experimentation, we found that a multiplier of 2-3 provides an appropriate
balance---avoiding excessive initial pipeline bubbles while ensuring that
subsequent chunks don't become too small as context length increases. With
the default dynamic chunking smoothing factor of 0.75, we performed
parameter tuning and determined that a value of 0.65 works optimally with
the 12K initial chunk size for the DeepSeek-V3.1, while a value of 0.8 works
optimally with the 18K initial chunk size for the Qwen3-235B-A22B-FP8.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------
Prefill Context Parallelism         *sglang-docs-advanced_features-prefill_cp*

Prefill context parallelism (CP) distributes the tokens of a prompt across
an attention CP group. Each rank computes attention and, for models with an
indexer, indexer operations for its local queries, while all-gather on the
KV cache makes the required keys and values available. This lets multiple
GPUs share the work of processing a long prompt.

To compare prefill CP with other common parallelism strategy: Tensor
parallelism (TP) splits attention heads and weights,
|sglang-docs-advanced_features-dcp| shards the KV cache and its attention
workload during decode, while prefill CP (PCP) splits prompt tokens across
GPUs. Note that PCP and DCP are independent optimizations for different
phases of inference.

           *docs-advanced_features-prefill_cp-why-prefill-context-parallelism*
WHY PREFILL CONTEXT PARALLELISM?

Prefill CP offers three benefits:

- It partitions work that would otherwise be repeated across ranks, such as
  indexer computation in DSA models and the DeepSeek V4 series.
- It combines naturally with KV-cache sharding to reduce per-rank cache
  memory. Layer-wise sharding is available through DSA cache LayerSplit;
  additional sharding techniques are under development.
- Combined with expert parallelism (EP), it can reduce communication time by
  using all-to-all token dispatch and combine instead of TP all-reduce. The
  benefit depends on the workload and interconnect.

ARCHITECTURE                  *docs-advanced_features-prefill_cp-architecture*

Strategy interface      *docs-advanced_features-prefill_cp-strategy-interface*

`ContextParallelStrategy` separates token-layout policy from model execution
and attention kernels. Server argument resolution initializes one strategy
per process. Per-forward state lives in `ForwardBatch.attn_cp_metadata`,
rather than in the model's token-layout logic.

Zigzag strategy            *docs-advanced_features-prefill_cp-zigzag-strategy*

For a CP group of size `C`, split each request's newly extended tokens into
`2C` contiguous blocks. Rank `r` receives block `r` and block `2C - 1 - r`.
The split restarts for every request in a batch.

For example, with CP=4 and 16 new tokens, each block has two tokens:

Pairing an early, cheaper block with a late, more expensive block balances
causal attention work while retaining contiguous query blocks. Lengths need
not divide evenly: early blocks receive the remainder, and communication
buffers are padded as needed.

The metadata records separate query and KV lengths for the early and late
blocks, including any cached prefix. Each block therefore attends to the
correct causal history, not just the other tokens assigned to its rank.

Interleave strategy    *docs-advanced_features-prefill_cp-interleave-strategy*

For CP size `C`, rank `r` receives flattened token indices
`r, r+C, r+2C, ...`. The index runs across the batch's newly extended
tokens; it does not reset at request boundaries. Position IDs keep their
original values.

With CP=4 and 16 new tokens:

This gives each rank queries spread across the context. For a batch
containing requests of lengths 5 and 3, rank 0 owns flattened indices 0 and
4, while rank 1 owns indices 1 and 5; index 5 is the first new token of the
second request. Per-request sharding metadata preserves those boundaries and
each query's causal extent.

             *docs-advanced_features-prefill_cp-attention-backend-integration*
Attention backend integration

Path                        Integration
--------------------------  --------------------------------------------------
Zigzag with FlashAttention  Gather and reorder new KV; execute attention for
                            the early and late query blocks with their
                            respective sequence lengths.
Zigzag with trtllm_mha      Materialize KV, build zigzag page tables, and
                            execute a combined variable-length attention call.
Interleave with DSA         Shard query/indexer metadata by request, gather
                            indexer keys and MLA KV as required, and execute
                            sparse attention in the backend.
DeepSeek V4 interleave      Uses model-specific sparse-attention integration;
                            the CP regression suite includes DeepSeek-V4-Flash
                            on B200. Do not infer its backend requirements
                            from the dense zigzag path.

The CP and attention-backend compatibility matrix is being expanded, with
support for more combinations planned.

COMPOSITIONS                  *docs-advanced_features-prefill_cp-compositions*

                   *docs-advanced_features-prefill_cp-prefill-cp-tp-dp-and-ep*
Prefill CP × TP, DP, and EP

Attention TP splits heads within each CP partition; attention DP separates
request batches. Dense FFNs and MoE layers can use a different layout,
bridged by the layer boundaries between stages (see Layer boundaries
https://docs.sglang.io/docs/developer_guide/layer_boundary). The Qwen3
example in |docs-advanced_features-prefill_cp-usage-and-examples| combines
CP=2 with attention TP=2 and EP=4. For interleave DSA on DeepSeek V3.2 and
the GLM-5 series, keep DP=1 and use the resolved attention CP=TP topology.

           *docs-advanced_features-prefill_cp-prefill-cp-pipeline-parallelism*
Prefill CP × pipeline parallelism

The eager runner preserves CP-local hidden states between pipeline stages
and gathers on the final stage. PP can place stages on different nodes while
keeping each DSA attention CP group within one node; it does not remove the
single-machine DSA CP restriction.

           *docs-advanced_features-prefill_cp-prefill-cp-speculative-decoding*
Prefill CP × speculative decoding

Prefill CP can coexist with supported speculative-decoding configurations.
The CP runner handles aligned speculative hidden-state inputs and gathers
supported auxiliary outputs.

                    *docs-advanced_features-prefill_cp-prefill-cp-cuda-graphs*
Prefill CP × CUDA graphs

The shared CP breakable-prefill-graph path currently requires `zigzag`, the
`trtllm_mha` prefill backend, PP=1, and attention CP size equal to TP size.
It uses CP-local static input buffers and selects capture buckets large
enough for each rank's padded input. Support for combining other attention
backends with prefill CP and Breakable CUDA Graph is under development.

*docs-advanced_features-prefill_cp-prefill-cp-pd-disaggregation-and-dsa-cache-layersplit*
Prefill CP × PD disaggregation and DSA cache LayerSplit

In supported DSA deployments, `--enable-dsa-cache-layer-split` distributes
GPU KV/indexer cache layers across CP ranks to reduce per-rank cache memory.
Each rank owns a range of layers and uses scratch storage for remote-layer
data. This is layer-wise cache ownership, separate from the interleave token
assignment used for computation, and is not applied to draft workers.

LayerSplit requires a PD prefill worker (`--disaggregation-mode prefill`),
`--enable-prefill-cp --cp-strategy interleave`, and PP=1. It currently
supports the `mooncake` and `mooncake_tcp` transfer backends. Do not enable
LayerSplit on decode or non-PD workers; the decode side receives full cache
shards through PD transfer. Use the
|sglang-docs-advanced_features-pd_disaggregation| and model-specific launch
recipes to configure both sides of the transfer; enabling prefill CP alone
does not configure a PD deployment.

USAGE AND EXAMPLES      *docs-advanced_features-prefill_cp-usage-and-examples*

Use NVIDIA CUDA GPUs and select a strategy supported by your model and
attention backend. The examples below target a single Linux host with Hopper
GPUs and an SGLang version that includes the selected backend.

Argument             Default  Description
-------------------  -------  ------------------------------------------------
--enable-prefill-cp  False    Enable context-parallel prefill.
--cp-strategy        Unset    Required when enabling prefill CP. Choose zigzag
                              or interleave.
--attn-cp-size       1        Number of ranks in an attention CP group. Use a
                              value greater than 1 to distribute work;
                              model-specific argument resolution may adjust
                              it.

CP subdivides the existing TP world; it does not add another GPU multiplier.
With attention DP enabled, the attention topology is:

>text
    TP world size = attention DP size × attention CP size × attention TP size

    Example: --tp 4 --dp 1 --attn-cp-size 2
             → one attention DP group, CP=2, attention TP=2
<
The server requires `--tp` to be divisible by `--dp × --attn-cp-size`. The
attention layout does not by itself specify the dense FFN or MoE layout;
those use their own parallelism settings.

  Warning: ~

  For DSA models, such as the GLM-5 series and DeepSeek V3.2, use
  `interleave`; `zigzag` is currently unavailable. Do not use a smaller
  `--attn-cp-size` to request hybrid attention TP/CP for DSA models. Broader
  compatibility is planned for future support.

*docs-advanced_features-prefill_cp-zigzag-example-gqa-with-attention-tp-and-cp*
Zigzag example: GQA with attention TP and CP

This Qwen3 configuration uses four Hopper GPUs, with attention TP=2, CP=2,
and EP=4 for the MoE layers. The model is a Hugging Face repository ID
passed to `--model-path`.

>sh
    python -m sglang.launch_server \
      --model-path Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP8 \
      --tp 4 \
      --ep 4 \
      --attn-cp-size 2 \
      --enable-prefill-cp \
      --cp-strategy zigzag \
      --attention-backend fa3
<

                    *docs-advanced_features-prefill_cp-interleave-example-dsa*
Interleave example: DSA

This GLM-5.2 configuration uses eight H200 GPUs with attention CP=8 and
attention TP=1. The DSA backend is selected automatically for this model;
the command makes that choice explicit.

>sh
    python -m sglang.launch_server \
      --model-path zai-org/GLM-5.2-FP8 \
      --tp 8 \
      --attn-cp-size 8 \
      --enable-prefill-cp \
      --cp-strategy interleave \
      --attention-backend dsa \
      --trust-remote-code \
      --mem-fraction-static 0.85
<
For model-specific deployment combinations, see
|autoregressive-GLM-GLM-5.3-3-5-context-parallelism|.

Quantization                      *sglang-docs-advanced_features-quantization*

SGLang supports various quantization methods, including offline quantization
and online dynamic quantization.

Offline quantization loads pre-quantized model weights directly during
inference. This is required for quantization methods such as GPTQ and AWQ,
which collect and pre-compute various statistics from the original weights
using the calibration dataset.

Online quantization dynamically computes scaling parameters---such as the
maximum/minimum values of model weights---during runtime. Like NVIDIA FP8
training's delayed scaling
https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/transformer-engine/user-guide/examples/fp8_primer.html#Mixed-precision-training-with-FP8
mechanism, online quantization calculates the appropriate scaling factors
on-the-fly to convert high-precision weights into a lower-precision format.

Note: For better performance, usability and convenience, offline
quantization is recommended over online quantization.

If you use a pre-quantized model, do not add `--quantization` to enable
online quantization at the same time. For popular pre-quantized models,
please visit Unsloth https://huggingface.co/unsloth, NVIDIA ModelOpt
https://huggingface.co/collections/nvidia/inference-optimized-checkpoints-with-model-optimizer
or NeuralMagic https://huggingface.co/collections/neuralmagic collections on
HF for some popular quality validated quantized models. Quantized models
must be validated via benchmarks post-quantization to guard against abnormal
quantization loss regressions.

  *docs-advanced_features-quantization-gemm-backends-for-fp4/fp8-quantization*
GEMM BACKENDS FOR FP4/FP8 QUANTIZATION

  Note: ~

  Backend selection applies to blockwise FP8, MXFP8 (dense linear), and
  NVFP4 GEMM. When running offline or online FP8 or FP4 quantized models,
  you can select the GEMM backend via `--fp8-gemm-backend` and
  `--fp4-gemm-backend`.

     *docs-advanced_features-quantization-fp8-gemm-backend-blockwise-fp8-gemm*
`--fp8-gemm-backend` (Blockwise FP8 GEMM)

Backend              Hardware     Description
-------------------  -----------  --------------------------------------------
auto                 All          Auto-selects based on hardware
deep_gemm            SM90, SM100  JIT-compiled; enabled when DeepGEMM is
                                  installed
flashinfer_trtllm    SM100        FlashInfer TensorRT-LLM backend; optimal for
                                  low-latency
flashinfer_cutlass   SM100/120    FlashInfer CUTLASS groupwise FP8 GEMM
flashinfer_deepgemm  SM90         Uses swapAB optimization for small M
                                  dimensions in decoding
cutlass              SM120        sgl-kernel CUTLASS
triton               All          Fallback; widely compatible
aiter                ROCm         AMD AITER backend

`auto` selection order: 1) DeepGEMM (SM90/SM100, installed); 2) FlashInfer
TRTLLM (SM100, FlashInfer available); 3) CUTLASS (SM120); 4) AITER (AMD); 5)
Triton (fallback).

MXFP8 dense linear: `auto` uses `flashinfer_cutlass` on SM100 (else
`triton`). `flashinfer_cutlass` is fastest on most shapes;
`flashinfer_trtllm` is faster only at small M.

MXFP8 dense linear, HALOps (opt-in): `--fp8-gemm-backend halops` routes
MXFP8 (group-32) dense linear GEMM through HALOps
https://github.com/PaddlePaddle/HALOps w8a8 kernels on SM100. The package is
published on PaddlePaddle's CUDA 13.2 package page rather than PyPI; the
official Docker image installs it, and outside Docker install it explicitly:

[Command]

[Command]Command

>sh
    uv pip install halops==0.1.0 \
      -f https://www.paddlepaddle.org.cn/packages/stable/cu132/halops/
<
The wheel is cp312 Linux only (x86_64 and aarch64); selecting the backend
without it raises an install hint.

Both quantization paths work: `--quantization mxfp8` on a BF16 checkpoint
(quantized at load), and a pre-quantized MXFP8 checkpoint, whose uint8 UE8M0
weight scales are used as they are.

*docs-advanced_features-quantization-tuned-tiles-for-per-token-x-per-channel-fp8*
Tuned tiles for per-token x per-channel FP8

Per-token activation x per-channel weight FP8 (for example
`compressed-tensors` W8A8 checkpoints) runs through `triton_scaled_mm`,
which can take a tile tuned per weight shape and M bucket instead of the
fixed dispatch. The tables are plain JSON under
`python/sglang/kernels/ops/gemm/configs/`, named
`N={N},K={K},device_name={DEVICE},dtype=fp8_w8a8_channelwise.json`; a bucket
set to `null` keeps the default dispatch. The lookup only matches the exact
device name, so any other GPU, or a shape with no table, keeps the default
dispatch unchanged. The file format is documented in
`python/sglang/kernels/ops/gemm/configs/README.md`.

             *docs-advanced_features-quantization-fp4-gemm-backend-nvfp4-gemm*
`--fp4-gemm-backend` (NVFP4 GEMM)

Backend             Hardware                      Description
------------------  ----------------------------  ----------------------------
auto                SM80+                         Auto-selects:
                                                  flashinfer_cutedsl on SM100;
                                                  marlin on SM80-SM90;
                                                  flashinfer_cutlass otherwise
                                                  (including SM120)
flashinfer_cutlass  SM100/120                     FlashInfer CUTLASS backend
flashinfer_cudnn    SM100/120 (CUDA 13+, cuDNN    FlashInfer cuDNN backend
                    9.15+)
flashinfer_cutedsl  SM100                         FlashInfer CuTe DSL backend
flashinfer_trtllm   SM100                         FlashInfer TensorRT-LLM
                                                  backend
marlin              SM80-SM90                     Weight-only W4A16 fallback
                                                  for NVFP4 checkpoints

On SM80-SM90, `auto` selects Marlin for NVFP4. NVFP4 GEMM requires
FlashInfer to be installed.

                    *docs-advanced_features-quantization-offline-quantization*
OFFLINE QUANTIZATION

To load already quantized models, simply load the model weights and config.
Again, if the model has been quantized offline, there's no need to add
`--quantization` argument when starting the engine. The quantization method
will be parsed from the downloaded Hugging Face or msModelSlim config. For
example, DeepSeek V3/R1 models are already in FP8, so do not add redundant
parameters.

[Command]

[Command]Command

>sh
    python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
        --model-path hugging-quants/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-AWQ-INT4 \
        --port 30000 --host 0.0.0.0
<
Take note, if your model is per-channel quantized (INT8 or FP8) with
per-token dynamic quantization activation, you can opt to include
`--quantization w8a8_int8` or `--quantization w8a8_fp8` to invoke the
corresponding CUTLASS int8_kernel or fp8_kernel in sgl-kernel. This action
will ignore the Hugging Face config's quantization settings. For instance,
with `neuralmagic/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-FP8-dynamic`, if you execute
with `--quantization w8a8_fp8`, the system will use the `W8A8Fp8Config` from
SGLang to invoke the sgl-kernel, rather than the `CompressedTensorsConfig`
for vLLM kernels.

[Command]

[Command]Command

>sh
    python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
        --model-path neuralmagic/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-FP8-dynamic \
        --quantization w8a8_fp8 \
        --port 30000 --host 0.0.0.0
<

[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    from sglang.srt.configs.load_config import LoadConfig
    from sglang.srt.configs.model_config import ModelConfig
    from sglang.srt.model_loader.loader import get_model_loader
    from sglang.srt.configs.device_config import DeviceConfig

    # Configure model with inc quantization and saving
    model_config = ModelConfig(
        model_path="meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct",
        quantization="auto-round-int8",
        trust_remote_code=True,
    )

    load_config = LoadConfig(
        inc_save_path="./quantized_model",
    )
    device_config = DeviceConfig(device="cpu")

    # Load and quantize the model
    model_loader = get_model_loader(load_config, model_config)
    quantized_model = model_loader.load_model(
        model_config=model_config,
        device_config=device_config,
    )
<
- known issues

Several limitations currently affect offline quantized model loading in
sglang, These issues might be resolved in future updates of sglang. If you
experience any problems, consider using Hugging Face Transformers as an
alternative.

1. Mixed-bit Quantization Limitations

   Mixed-bit quantization is not fully supported. Due to vLLM's layer fusion
   (e.g., QKV fusion), applying different bit-widths to components within
   the same fused layer can lead to compatibility issues.
2. Limited Support for Quantized MoE Models

   Quantized MoE models may encounter inference issues due to kernel
   limitations (e.g., lack of support for mlp.gate layer quantization).
   please try to skip quantizing these layers to avoid such errors.
3. Limited Support for Quantized VLMs

   Details                          *docs-advanced_features-quantization-details*

     Qwen2.5-VL-7B

     auto_round:auto_gptq format: Accuracy is close to zero.

     GPTQ format: Fails with:

     [Output]

     [Output]Output

     >text
         The output size is not aligned with the quantized weight shape
<
     auto_round:auto_awq and AWQ format: These work as expected.

4. Limited Support for SGlang API Usage

   SGlang API Usage only supports `auto-round-int8` quantization method now,
   more quantization methods are on the way.

- CPU serving

  AutoRound INT4 checkpoints (both `auto_round:auto_gptq` and
  `auto_round:auto_awq` packing formats) can be served on Intel CPUs with
  AMX support:

  >sh
      SGLANG_USE_CPU_ENGINE=1 python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
          --model-path OPEA/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct-int4-sym-inc \
          --quantization auto-round \
          --device cpu --trust-remote-code
<
  The current SGLang CPU backend supports only 4-bit AutoRound checkpoints
  on Intel AMX. Other AutoRound bit-widths and non-AMX CPU backends are not
  supported by this path.

>python
    from datasets import load_dataset
    from gptqmodel import GPTQModel, QuantizeConfig

    model_id = "meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct"
    quant_path = "Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-gptqmodel-4bit"

        "allenai/c4", data_files="en/c4-train.00001-of-01024.json.gz",
        split="train"
      ).select(range(1024))["text"]
