----------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                *sglang-docs-advanced_features-unified_memory*
Unified Memory for Hybrid Models

A hybrid model stores more than one kind of per-request memory:
full-attention KV, sliding-window (SWA) KV, and recurrent state for Mamba or
linear-attention layers. By default SGLang gives each kind its own pool and
fixes the split at startup (`--swa-full-tokens-ratio`,
`--mamba-full-memory-ratio`). When the workload does not match that split,
one pool runs out while the other has room to spare.

With `--enable-unified-memory`, every kind lives in one device buffer, the
arena. Each kind is a sub-pool that occupies a contiguous band of the
arena's bytes, and bands grow and shrink as requests come and go. Memory
moves between kinds as the workload shifts: long prompts take more
full-attention KV, many short concurrent requests take more state slots and
window KV.

This page covers when and how to enable it. The design page
https://docs.sglang.io/docs/advanced_features/unified_memory_design
describes how it works and how to debug and test it.

WHAT CHANGES              *docs-advanced_features-unified_memory-what-changes*

               Separate pools (default)        Unified memory
-------------  ------------------------------  -------------------------------
Device memory  One buffer per pool, split by   One arena; every sub-pool takes
               ratios at startup               pages from it at run time
Capacity       Fixed per kind; one kind can    Shared; every capacity decision
               be full while another is idle   asks whether one layout of the
                                               arena serves a concrete demand.
                                               Per-sub-pool availability
                                               figures are estimates for
                                               observers
Token ids      req_to_token holds the ids the  req_to_token holds virtual ids;
               kernels index                   each sub-pool maps them to
                                               physical pages, so pages can
                                               move without rewriting request
                                               tables
KV layout      One buffer per layer            Page-major entries: one entry
                                               per token slot (or state slot)
                                               holds every layer's rows, so
                                               --enable-page-major-kv-layout
                                               is implied
Compaction     None                            Pages move lazily to close
                                               holes and make room, ordered
                                               behind the forwards and
                                               transfers that may still touch
                                               them

                   *docs-advanced_features-unified_memory-sub-pools-and-bands*
Sub-pools and bands

Each kind of memory a model's layers declare becomes one sub-pool:

Sub-pool         Name                 Holds                Unit
---------------  -------------------  -------------------  -------------------
Full attention   full                 The full-attention   A page of
                                      KV. It owns the      --page-size tokens
                                      token id space.
Sliding window   window_<length>,     The KV of layers     A page
                 for example          that attend through
                 window_4096 (window  one window length
                 when the model does
                 not state the
                 length)
Recurrent state  mamba                One state entry per  One slot
                                      slot (conv and SSM
                                      state of every
                                      state layer)

With DSA sparse attention, each page of the `full` sub-pool holds its
tokens' FP8 latent rows (with block scales) layer by layer, then each
indexer layer's keys for those tokens, as the paged indexer kernels read
them.

Sub-pools are laid out in the arena by retention: the state sub-pool takes
the low end and grows up, the full-attention sub-pool takes the high end and
grows down, and window sub-pools sit between them. With no state sub-pool,
the longest window takes the low end. A sub-pool between the two ends is a
float: it occupies a span between its neighbours and is relocated when the
layout needs it.

>text
    low byte                                                                  high byte
    | sink | mamba ->          | <- window_4096 -> |                 <- full |
             grow-up end          float                                grow-down end
<
The low bytes are a padding sink that every sub-pool's dummy writes land in.

SUPPORTED MODELS      *docs-advanced_features-unified_memory-supported-models*

Unified memory replaces the pools of hybrid models only. At startup,
`KVCacheConfigurator._kv_layer_decls` declares the model's layers and
refuses anything else.

Model family                        Supported
----------------------------------  ------------------------------------------
Hybrid sliding-window attention     Yes
with MHA full attention (for
example gpt-oss, Gemma 4)
Hybrid Mamba or linear attention    Yes
(for example Qwen3-Next and
Qwen3.5 GDN models, Kimi Linear
with MLA)
Sliding window and recurrent state  Yes
together
Full attention only (plain MHA or   No: refused at startup
MLA)
MLA full attention with             No
sliding-window layers
DeepSeek-V4 (compressed-KV          No
attention)
MLA with DSA sparse attention and   Yes, with the flashmla_kv DSA backends;
recurrent state (Kimi-K3.1)         not yet with speculative decoding,
                                    --dcp-size, PD disaggregation,
                                    hierarchical cache or
                                    --enable-return-indexer-topk
Qwen4-Exp, Unlimited-OCR v2,        No: refused by their model overrides
MiniCPM with its sparse attention
backends

The target model's sliding-window layers form one window sub-pool. A fused
draft model whose window has a different length adds a second one. Only the
Triton attention backend serves several window sub-pools per runner; another
backend bound to more windows than it supports raises at startup, naming
itself.

*docs-advanced_features-unified_memory-attention-linear-attention-and-mamba-backends*
Attention, linear-attention and Mamba backends

Page-major entries make each layer's rows strided, so only backends audited
for strided views are accepted. The table is that page-major allow-list
(`arg_groups/kv_cache_hook.py::handle_page_major_kv_layout`); a backend on
it may still refuse a model when it is built:

Layers                              Page-major allow-list
----------------------------------  ------------------------------------------
MHA full and sliding-window         triton, fa3, fa4, flashinfer, trtllm_mha
attention
MHA with asymmetric K/V head dims   triton, fa3, fa4
MLA full attention                  triton, fa3, trtllm_mla, flashinfer,
                                    cutedsl_mla, flashmla; dsa for
                                    sparse-attention models, with the
                                    flashmla_kv prefill and decode backends
Linear attention, decode            triton, flashinfer; also cutedsl and
                                    helion on MLA (KDA) hybrids
Linear attention, prefill           triton, flashkda, flashinfer; also cutedsl
                                    and helion on MLA (KDA) hybrids
Mamba (--mamba-backend)             triton

`fa3` and `fa4` still refuse two kinds of model when the backend is built:
local-attention models, such as Llama 4, whose default backend on SM90 is
`fa3` (`FlashAttentionBackend._maybe_init_local_attn_builder`), and models
that decode with prefill-aware SWA (`FlashAttentionBackend.__init__`).

If the FULL prefill CUDA-graph backend is configured with an attention
backend other than `fa3` or `fa4`, it is disabled with a warning; decode
capture and the other prefill graph backends are unaffected.

QUICK START                *docs-advanced_features-unified_memory-quick-start*

Platform: NVIDIA CUDA. On other platforms, read
|docs-advanced_features-unified_memory-known-limitations| first.

>sh
    python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
      --model-path MODEL_PATH \
      --tp 2 \
      --enable-unified-memory
<
`MODEL_PATH` is a Hugging Face repo id or local path of a supported hybrid
model.

       *docs-advanced_features-unified_memory-flags-and-environment-variables*
FLAGS AND ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES

Flag or variable                      Effect under unified memory
------------------------------------  ----------------------------------------
--enable-unified-memory               Builds the arena, the per-sub-pool views
                                      and one allocator over all of them.
                                      Implies --enable-page-major-kv-layout.
--mem-fraction-static                 The arena's byte budget comes from the
                                      static memory fraction, as for separate
                                      pools. If the arena cannot hold the
                                      floor of one request at batch size 1
                                      (its window rows, its state slots and
                                      the sink), startup fails and names the
                                      terms (kv/sizing.py::check_bs1_floor).
                                      Whether a whole request fits, its
                                      full-attention tokens included, is
                                      checked at the memory clip and at
                                      admission.
--max-total-tokens                    Sizes the arena: its bytes are the
                                      smallest budget, within the measured
                                      one, whose sizing gives at least that
                                      many full-attention tokens, with windows
                                      and state sized by the same rules. It
                                      sizes the full-attention target; it does
                                      not cap how far full attention can grow
                                      into the arena at run time.
--max-running-requests                Bounds the concurrency the sizing solves
                                      for. The result is also capped at half
                                      the full-attention tokens.
--swa-full-tokens-ratio               Sets the window sub-pools' sizing target
                                      relative to full attention. It is a boot
                                      target, not a partition.
--mamba-full-memory-ratio,            Set the state sub-pool's boot target: a
--max-mamba-cache-size                share of the arena, or an explicit slot
                                      count. The arena may give state more
                                      slots at run time.
--radix-eviction-policy joint_lru     On full/SWA hybrids with exactly one
                                      window sub-pool and no state sub-pool,
                                      evicts full-attention and window KV in
                                      one shared least-recently-used order;
                                      elsewhere, several windows included,
                                      each component is evicted in its own
                                      least-recently-used order. See radix
                                      eviction policies.
SGLANG_DISABLE_LAZY_COMPACTION        Must stay unset: unified memory requires
                                      lazy compaction and refuses to start
                                      with it set.
SGLANG_LAZY_COMPACTION_MAX_MOVES_PER_CALL  Caps the page moves of one opportunistic
                                      compaction pass per band, so a large
                                      backlog does not stall the scheduler
                                      loop. Urgent compaction is uncapped.
SGLANG_LOG_LAZY_COMPACTION_STATS,     Log per-sub-pool compaction statistics
SGLANG_LOG_LAZY_COMPACTION_STATS_INTERVAL_SEC  periodically.
SGLANG_ENABLE_WAR_BARRIER             Not needed: unified memory turns the
                                      scheduler's write-after-read barrier on,
                                      on every device.
SGLANG_ENABLE_POST_CAPTURE_KV_SIZING  Sizes the arena after CUDA-graph capture
                                      and grows its backing in place (CUDA
                                      only).

A prompt that cannot fit even an otherwise empty arena is aborted at
admission with `Request prompt exceeds the KV memory budget`. The memory
clip and admission price a request with the same demand model
(`ChainAllocator.max_new_tokens_for_memory`). On a model with sliding-window
and Mamba layers whose cache keeps state checkpoints, its window bound
assumes the checkpoints advance; when no tracking or replacement state slot
is free, a request can hold more window rows than it was priced for, so
passing the clip does not guarantee that its chunks finish (see
|docs-advanced_features-unified_memory-known-limitations|).

       *docs-advanced_features-unified_memory-interaction-with-other-features*
INTERACTION WITH OTHER FEATURES

Feature                             Status under unified memory
----------------------------------  ------------------------------------------
Overlap scheduler                   Supported (the default). Freed pages stay
                                    pending until the forwards that may still
                                    touch them are processed.
Radix cache                         Supported, with one prefix-tree slot per
                                    sub-pool. On a model with sliding-window
                                    and Mamba layers whose cache keeps state
                                    checkpoints (--mamba-radix-cache-strategy
                                    extra_buffer), a prefill frees window rows
                                    only behind its latest checkpoint, so
                                    every prefill chunk but a prompt's last is
                                    cut on the checkpoint grid, and a
                                    --chunked-prefill-size below that grid is
                                    refused at startup.
HiCache                             Supported, with one host pool per sub-pool
(--enable-hierarchical-cache)       (the two end sub-pools may share one host
                                    backing when both hold MHA pages).
                                    --hicache-mem-layout page_first_direct is
                                    switched to page_first with the kernel I/O
                                    backend, because the direct copies assume
                                    packed rows. Not supported together with
                                    EAGLE/EAGLE3. With --pp-size above 1,
                                    --hicache-host-memory-mode buffer_only is
                                    refused: each stage drains its own backup
                                    completions, so the stages' eviction
                                    credit, and with it their capacity
                                    decisions, could differ.
PD disaggregation                   Supported with
                                    --disaggregation-transfer-backend mooncake
                                    or nixl. NIXL currently requires CUDA and
                                    the UCX backend; use this version on both
                                    peers. Refused with: --pp-size above 1,
                                    speculative decoding,
                                    SGLANG_DISAGG_STAGING_BUFFER
                                    (heterogeneous-TP staging),
                                    --enable-hisparse, and --dcp-size above 1.
                                    Prefill and decode must both enable
                                    unified memory, with the same attention TP
                                    size (with or without the staging buffer),
                                    page size and model. Decode KV offload
                                    needs --hicache-storage-backend file and
                                    does not support MLA, Mamba or
                                    sliding-window models.
                                    --disaggregation-decode-retraction-backup
                                    host_pool does not support Mamba models.
Speculative decoding                EAGLE, EAGLE3 (NEXTN resolves to EAGLE),
                                    DFLASH and DSPARK, with
                                    --speculative-eagle-topk unset or 1.
                                    EAGLE/EAGLE3 needs a hybrid target: the
                                    draft's KV lives inside the target's
                                    sub-pool entries. Other algorithms,
                                    including the Gemma 4 assistant draft's
                                    frozen-KV MTP, are refused.
Pipeline parallelism                Runs without PD disaggregation. Each stage
                                    sizes its own arena, and the stages agree
                                    on the minimum of their concurrency
                                    limits. At startup they exchange their
                                    arena geometry; each stage then answers
                                    every capacity question from every stage's
                                    geometry and the request state they share,
                                    so all stages make the same decisions.
                                    Every stage needs a full-attention layer,
                                    which owns the virtual ids, and all stages
                                    must plan the same sub-pools on the same
                                    page size: a layer partition that leaves a
                                    stage without full-attention layers, or
                                    with a layer kind or window length another
                                    stage lacks, is refused.
                                    --enable-streaming-session and
                                    --enable-session-radix-cache are refused
                                    too: each stage closes timed-out sessions
                                    on its own clock, so the memory the stages
                                    hold could differ. See Known limitations.
Decode context parallelism          MLA models only (for example Kimi Linear),
(--dcp-size above 1)                no sliding-window layers, no PD
                                    disaggregation, and attention backends
                                    flashinfer, trtllm_mla or cutedsl_mla.
                                    With speculative decoding, the backend
                                    that runs target verification must be
                                    cutedsl_mla: the decode backend with
                                    --speculative-attention-mode decode,
                                    otherwise the prefill backend. With DSPARK
                                    or DFLASH, flashinfer is refused.
Data-parallel attention             Each attention-DP rank has its own arena.

Refused at startup:

- `--enable-two-batch-overlap`
- `--enable-lmcache`, `--enable-unified-cache-external-linker`
- `--enable-kv-cache-sharding`
- `--enable-int8-mamba-checkpoint`
- `--enable-prefill-weight-versions`
- FP4 KV cache (`--kv-cache-dtype nvfp4` or `fp4_mx_block16`)
- `--cp-kv-layout` values that keep each rank's KV sharded and padded
- out-of-tree platforms

OBSERVABILITY            *docs-advanced_features-unified_memory-observability*

Pool usage is reported per sub-pool: each window sub-pool has its own label,
and state is reported in slots. Because sub-pools share bytes, the available
figures are estimates; the held figures are exact. At idle, the scheduler
checks every sub-pool for leaked pages and the arena for byte conservation.
The design page
https://docs.sglang.io/docs/advanced_features/unified_memory_design#debugging-and-testing
lists the stricter checks and the test tools.

KNOWN LIMITATIONS    *docs-advanced_features-unified_memory-known-limitations*

- Priority preemption. With `--enable-priority-scheduling`, unified memory
  turns priority preemption off, with a startup warning: a higher-priority
  request is admitted first but does not retract running requests, so under
  load it waits for running requests to finish.
- MPS and MLX. Refused at startup: unified memory orders the scheduler's
  writes after the running forward's reads with device stream waits, and the
  scheduler has no device streams there.
- Window rows when state checkpoints stall. On a model with sliding-window
  and Mamba layers whose cache keeps state checkpoints, the memory clip and
  admission assume each request's checkpoints advance. When no tracking or
  replacement state slot is free, a checkpoint stalls and the request holds
  more window rows than it was priced for, so an admitted request is not
  guaranteed to finish. See the checkpoint retention bound
  https://docs.sglang.io/docs/advanced_features/unified_memory_design#known-limitations.
- PD failed transfers. A failed or timed-out transfer's pages are released
  at its deferred-release timeout, or a failed send's at once, without proof
  that the remote transfer engine stopped touching them.

The design page
https://docs.sglang.io/docs/advanced_features/unified_memory_design#known-limitations
names the code paths.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------
Query VLM with Offline Engine        *sglang-docs-advanced_features-vlm_query*

This tutorial demonstrates how to use SGLang's offline Engine API to query
VLMs. We will demonstrate usage with Qwen2.5-VL and Llama 4. This section
demonstrates three different calling approaches:

1. Basic Call: Directly pass images and text.
2. Processor Output: Use HuggingFace processor for data preprocessing.
3. Precomputed Embeddings: Pre-calculate image features to improve inference
   efficiency.

      *docs-advanced_features-vlm_query-understanding-the-three-input-formats*
UNDERSTANDING THE THREE INPUT FORMATS

SGLang supports three ways to pass visual data, each optimized for different
scenarios:

             *docs-advanced_features-vlm_query-1-raw-images-simplest-approach*
1. Raw Images - Simplest approach

- Pass PIL Images, file paths, URLs, or base64 strings directly
- SGLang handles all preprocessing automatically
- Best for: Quick prototyping, simple applications

*docs-advanced_features-vlm_query-2-processor-output-for-custom-preprocessing*
2. Processor Output - For custom preprocessing

- Pre-process images with HuggingFace processor
- Pass the complete processor output dict with `format: "processor_output"`
- Best for: Custom image transformations, integration with existing
  pipelines
- Requirement: Must use `input_ids` instead of text prompt

*docs-advanced_features-vlm_query-3-precomputed-embeddings-for-maximum-performance*
3. Precomputed Embeddings - For maximum performance

- Pre-calculate visual embeddings using the vision encoder
- Pass embeddings with `format: "precomputed_embedding"`
- Best for: Repeated queries on same images, caching, high-throughput
  serving
- Performance gain: Avoids redundant vision encoder computation (30-50%
  speedup)

Key Rule: Within a single request, use only one format for all images. Don't
mix formats.

The examples below demonstrate all three approaches with both Qwen2.5-VL and
Llama 4 models.

                  *docs-advanced_features-vlm_query-multimodal-cache-identity*
MULTIMODAL CACHE IDENTITY

SGLang identifies actual media features or supplied embeddings using full
256-bit digests. Cache identities also include tensor shape and dtype,
container boundaries, modality, model-specific metadata, and the effective
model/processor configuration. CPU and CUDA tensor hashing use BLAKE3; GPU
hashing transfers only the digests to the host. These are
collision-resistant identifiers, not a mathematical guarantee that
collisions are impossible.

- `mm_hashes` remains accepted for compatibility, but cannot override cache
  keys or skip server-side content hashing. External routers must not assume
  that a supplied scalar hash equals SGLang's internal KV-cache key.
- `mm_content_hashes` describes source content. Keep
  `--trust-mm-content-hashes` disabled for untrusted clients; enabling it
  allows preprocessing-cache lookup before verifying the supplied media.
- Embedding caching and batch deduplication retain the full identity. KV
  caching namespaces each request by its ordered media identities and
  `cache_salt`, so a short placeholder collision cannot reuse another
  image's KV state. Requests with identical media can still share prefixes;
  requests with different media do not share even their common text prefix.
  This can increase prefill cost for workloads with long shared instructions
  and changing images.
- Pin model revisions when sharing encoder caches. Clear caches or restart
  when replacing weights or processor implementations in place; a
  configuration fingerprint is not a checksum of all model weights.

Custom processors must hash the final model-facing features and metadata
before exporting CUDA transport handles. The shared frontend finalization
path then binds the processor namespace and updates any prebuilt padding
together; composite processors must delegate this step to their inner
processor. Keep server-created full identities intact across transport and
never use a truncated scalar hash as an embedding or KV-cache identity.

                 *docs-advanced_features-vlm_query-call-with-processor-output*
Call with Processor Output

Using a HuggingFace processor to preprocess text and images, and passing the
`processor_output` directly into `Engine.generate`.

[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    from transformers import AutoProcessor

    processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_path)
    processor_output = processor(
        images=[image], text=conv.get_prompt(), return_tensors="pt"
    )

    out = llm.generate(
        input_ids=processor_output["input_ids"][0].detach().cpu().tolist(),
        image_data=[dict(processor_output, format="processor_output")],
    )
    print("Response using processor output:")
    print(out["text"])

           *docs-advanced_features-vlm_query-call-with-precomputed-embeddings*
Call with Precomputed Embeddings

You can pre-calculate image features to avoid repeated visual encoding
processes.

[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    from transformers import AutoProcessor
    from transformers import Qwen2_5_VLForConditionalGeneration

    processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_path)
    model = Qwen2_5_VLForConditionalGeneration.from_pretrained(model_path).eval()
    vision = model.model.visual.cuda()
<
[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    processor_output = processor(
        images=[image], text=conv.get_prompt(), return_tensors="pt"
    )

    input_ids = processor_output["input_ids"][0].detach().cpu().tolist()

    precomputed_embeddings = vision(
        processor_output["pixel_values"].cuda(), processor_output["image_grid_thw"].cuda()
    )
    precomputed_embeddings = precomputed_embeddings.pooler_output

    multi_modal_item = dict(
        processor_output,
        format="precomputed_embedding",
        feature=precomputed_embeddings,
    )

    out = llm.generate(input_ids=input_ids, image_data=[multi_modal_item])
    print("Response using precomputed embeddings:")
    print(out["text"])

    llm.shutdown()

    from transformers import AutoProcessor

    processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_path)
    processor_output = processor(
        images=[image], text=conv.get_prompt(), return_tensors="pt"
    )

    out = llm.generate(
        input_ids=processor_output["input_ids"][0].detach().cpu().tolist(),

         *docs-advanced_features-vlm_query-call-with-precomputed-embeddings-2*
Call with Precomputed Embeddings

[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    from transformers import AutoProcessor
    from transformers import Llama4ForConditionalGeneration

    processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_path)
    model = Llama4ForConditionalGeneration.from_pretrained(
        model_path, torch_dtype="auto"
    ).eval()

    vision = model.vision_model.cuda()
    multi_modal_projector = model.multi_modal_projector.cuda()

    print(f'Image pixel values shape: {processor_output["pixel_values"].shape}')
    input_ids = processor_output["input_ids"][0].detach().cpu().tolist()

    # Process image through vision encoder
    image_outputs = vision(
        processor_output["pixel_values"].to("cuda"),
        aspect_ratio_ids=processor_output["aspect_ratio_ids"].to("cuda"),
        aspect_ratio_mask=processor_output["aspect_ratio_mask"].to("cuda"),
        output_hidden_states=False
    )
    image_features = image_outputs.last_hidden_state

    # Flatten image features and pass through multimodal projector
    vision_flat = image_features.view(-1, image_features.size(-1))
    precomputed_embeddings = multi_modal_projector(vision_flat)

    # Build precomputed embedding data item
    mm_item = dict(
        processor_output,
        format="precomputed_embedding",
        feature=precomputed_embeddings
    )

    # Use precomputed embeddings for efficient inference
    out = llm.generate(input_ids=input_ids, image_data=[mm_item])
    print("Llama 4 precomputed embedding response:")
    print(out["text"])
<

----------------------------------------------------------------------------
Anthropic-Compatible API               *sglang-docs-basic_usage-anthropic_api*

Use the Anthropic Messages API (/v1/messages) with SGLang, including Claude
Code integration and prefix-cache tuning.

SGLang ships an Anthropic-compatible `/v1/messages` endpoint so any client
built for the Anthropic Messages API --- including the Anthropic SDKs and
agentic CLIs such as Claude Code --- can talk to a self-hosted SGLang server
without changes. A complete reference for the API is available in the
Anthropic API Reference https://docs.anthropic.com/en/api/messages.

The endpoint is registered automatically on every SGLang server; no extra
flag is required to enable it. It reuses the same model, chat template, and
reasoning / tool-call parsers as the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, and
supports both non-streaming and streaming responses, tool use, and a
`count_tokens` route.

This tutorial covers:

- `POST /v1/messages` (non-streaming and streaming)
- `POST /v1/messages/count_tokens`
- Pointing Claude Code at the server, including the
  `CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER` setting that is required for good
  prefix-cache reuse.

LAUNCH A SERVER               *docs-basic_usage-anthropic_api-launch-a-server*

Launch the server in your terminal and wait for it to initialize. The
Anthropic `/v1/messages` endpoint is registered automatically --- no extra
flag is required beyond the usual server launch. The example below is a
single-node GLM-5.2-FP8 config; see the |sglang-autoregressive-GLM-GLM-5.2|
for verified commands across hardware and quantizations.

[Command]

[Command]Command

>sh
    sglang serve \
        --model-path zai-org/GLM-5.2-FP8 \
        --tp 8 \
        --speculative-algorithm EAGLE \
        --speculative-num-steps 5 \
        --speculative-eagle-topk 1 \
        --speculative-num-draft-tokens 6 \
        --reasoning-parser glm45 \
        --tool-call-parser glm47 \
        --host 0.0.0.0 \
        --port 30000
<
  Note: ~

  - The endpoint is model-agnostic. The `/v1/messages` route is on by
    default for any model; GLM-5.2 is used here because its reasoning +
    tool-use output is where Claude Code integration shines, but any model
    works.
  - Model name and `[1m]`. SGLang does not validate the request `model`
    field, so Claude Code can send any name. The `[1m]` suffix is a
    client-side hint: Claude Code only enables its 1M-context beta when the
    model name ends in `[1m]` --- without it, context is capped. Set the
    same `glm-5.2[1m]` in the `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_*_MODEL` env vars below.
  - `--reasoning-parser` / `--tool-call-parser` are optional. Add them when
    the model emits reasoning content (GLM-5.2, Qwen3, DeepSeek-R1, ...) or
    when you want tool calls parsed into structured `tool_use` blocks.
    Without a tool-call parser, tool schemas are still accepted but the
    model's tool calls come back as raw text, and Claude Code cannot execute
    them.
  - Context length defaults to the model's own (1M for GLM-5.2); pass
    `--context-length` only to cap it.

SEND A MESSAGE                 *docs-basic_usage-anthropic_api-send-a-message*

Non-Streaming                   *docs-basic_usage-anthropic_api-non-streaming*

Use the Anthropic Python SDK pointed at the server. Unlike the OpenAI SDK,
the Anthropic SDK appends `/v1/messages` itself, so `base_url` is the server
root without a `/v1` suffix.

[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    from anthropic import Anthropic

    client = Anthropic(
        base_url="http://127.0.0.1:30000",
        api_key="EMPTY",  # SGLang does not require a real key by default
    )

    message = client.messages.create(
        model="zai-org/GLM-5.2-FP8",
        max_tokens=512,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "List 3 countries and their capitals."}],
    )
    # A reasoning model may emit a `thinking` block before the `text` block —
    # pick the text block rather than assuming content[0].
    print(next(b.text for b in message.content if b.type == "text"))
<
Example Output:

[Output]

[Output]Output

>text
    Here are 3 countries and their capitals:

    1. **France** - Paris
    2. **Japan** - Tokyo
    3. **Brazil** - Brasília
<

>python
    with client.messages.stream(
        model="zai-org/GLM-5.2-FP8",
        max_tokens=512,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Say this is a test"}],
    ) as stream:
        for text in stream.text_stream:
            print(text, end="", flush=True)

Tool Use                             *docs-basic_usage-anthropic_api-tool-use*

Tool definitions follow the Anthropic `tools` schema. When the server is
launched with a `--tool-call-parser`, the model's tool calls are returned as
`tool_use` content blocks:

[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    message = client.messages.create(
        model="zai-org/GLM-5.2-FP8",
        max_tokens=512,
        tools=[
            {
                "name": "get_weather",
                "description": "Get the weather for a city",
                "input_schema": {
                    "type": "object",
                    "properties": {"city": {"type": "string"}},
                    "required": ["city"],
                },
            }
        ],
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What is the weather in Paris?"}],
    )
    print(message.stop_reason)
    print([b for b in message.content if b.type == "tool_use"])
<
Example Output:

[Output]

[Output]Output

>text
    tool_use
    [ToolUseBlock(type='tool_use', id='toolu_01XXXX', name='get_weather', input={'city': 'Paris'})]
<

Counting Tokens               *docs-basic_usage-anthropic_api-counting-tokens*

`POST /v1/messages/count_tokens` returns the tokenized length of a request
without generating a response. It reuses the same request conversion as
`/v1/messages`, so system prompts, tools, and multi-turn history are all
accounted for.

[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    resp = client.messages.count_tokens(
        model="zai-org/GLM-5.2-FP8",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello, world"}],
    )
    print(resp.input_tokens)
<
Example Output:

[Output]

[Output]Output

>text
    15

USING CLAUDE CODE           *docs-basic_usage-anthropic_api-using-claude-code*

Claude Code can be pointed at an SGLang server by setting a few env vars in
the shell that starts it. With the server already running on `:30000`,
export the full set and launch `claude`:

[Command]

[Command]Command

>sh
    export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL="http://127.0.0.1:30000"
    export ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN="dummy"                 # required by Claude Code; any non-empty string works
    export API_TIMEOUT_MS="3000000"                     # long timeout — reasoning + 1M-context turns are slow
    export CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW="1000000"     # let auto-compact use the full 1M window
    export CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC=1   # drop autoupdater/telemetry/error-reporting noise
    export CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER=0             # required for prefix-cache reuse — see below
    export ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL="glm-5.2[1m]"    # [1m] suffix enables Claude Code's 1M-context beta
    export ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL="glm-5.2[1m]"  # [1m] suffix enables Claude Code's 1M-context beta
    export ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL="glm-5.2[1m]"     # [1m] suffix enables Claude Code's 1M-context beta
    claude
<
Each var matters:

- `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` --- points Claude Code at your SGLang server instead
  of the Anthropic API.
- `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` --- Claude Code requires a non-empty auth token;
  SGLang accepts any value when launched without `--api-key`.
- `API_TIMEOUT_MS` --- raise it; reasoning models with long outputs and
  1M-context turns routinely exceed the default timeout.
- `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_{HAIKU,SONNET,OPUS}_MODEL` --- the model name Claude
  Code sends for each tier. SGLang does not validate this field, so any name
  works. Use `glm-5.2[1m]`: the `[1m]` suffix is a client-side hint that
  enables Claude Code's 1M-context beta (without it, context is capped).
- `CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW` --- set to `1000000` so auto-compaction
  uses the full 1M window instead of the default, keeping long sessions
  alive.

  Tip: ~

  Instead of exporting these in every shell, persist them in
  `~/.claude/settings.json` under the `env` key --- they apply to all Claude
  Code sessions:

  >json
      {
        "env": {
          "ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL": "http://127.0.0.1:30000",
          "ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN": "dummy",
          "CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC": "1",
          "CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER": "0",
          "ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL": "glm-5.2[1m]",
          "ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL": "glm-5.2[1m]",
          "ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL": "glm-5.2[1m]"
        }
      }
<

*docs-basic_usage-anthropic_api-required-claude_code_attribution_header=0-for-prefix-cache-reuse*
Required: `CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER=0` for prefix-cache reuse

  Note: ~

  Set this whenever Claude Code routes through SGLang (or any non-Anthropic
  gateway). Without it, multi-turn conversations re-prefill the whole
  history every turn.

Claude Code prepends a per-request attribution block to the start of the
system prompt, of the form
`x-anthropic-billing-header: cc_version=<ver>.<per-request-hash>; cc_entrypoint=...; cch=<hash>;`.
The per-request hash is the first token to differ between turns, so the
radix prefix cache can only reuse the short prefix before that hash and
re-prefills the system prompt plus the entire conversation history on every
turn.

Setting `CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER=0` removes the whole attribution
line from the system prompt. This is a documented Claude Code env var whose
explicit purpose is to “improve prompt-cache hit rates when routing through
an LLM gateway https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway” (see the
Claude Code env-vars reference https://code.claude.com/docs/en/env-vars).

  Note: ~

  `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC` does not remove the attribution
  block --- it only covers autoupdater/telemetry/error reporting. The
  attribution header is a separate code path; use
  `CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER=0` for it.

TROUBLESHOOTING               *docs-basic_usage-anthropic_api-troubleshooting*

Connection refused / `fetch failed` --- Ensure the server is up and the port
in `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` matches `--port` (default 30000). If you set
`ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` to a remote host, confirm it's reachable and not behind
a proxy that blocks the connection.

`Model not found` / 404 from the server --- SGLang does not validate the
request `model` field and serves whatever model was loaded at startup, so a
404 usually means the request did not reach the `/v1/messages` route at all.
Confirm `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` points at the server (not missing the port) and
that the server finished loading.

Tool calls not working / returned as raw text --- Launch the server with the
correct `--tool-call-parser` for your model (e.g. `glm47`, `qwen3`). Without
it the `tools` field is still accepted but the model's tool calls come back
as text instead of `tool_use` blocks, and Claude Code cannot execute them.

Slow / re-prefills the whole history every turn --- You are missing
`CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER=0`. Claude Code's per-request attribution
hash in the system prompt defeats radix prefix-cache reuse; see the section
above.

Context capped below 1M --- The model name must end in `[1m]` for Claude
Code to enable its 1M-context beta. Verify `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_*_MODEL` uses
the `[1m]` suffix, and that the loaded model's native context is 1M (GLM-5.2
is 1048576; pass `--context-length` only to cap it, not to extend).

PARAMETERS                         *docs-basic_usage-anthropic_api-parameters*

The `/v1/messages` endpoint accepts the standard Anthropic Messages API
parameters. Refer to the Anthropic Messages API reference
https://docs.anthropic.com/en/api/messages for the full list.

Reasoning models are supported through the same `--reasoning-parser`
mechanism as the OpenAI-compatible endpoint; pass the model's reasoning
kwarg via the request (e.g. `thinking` for DeepSeek-V3-style models,
`enable_thinking` for Qwen3-style models). See
|sglang-docs-basic_usage-openai_api_completions| for the reasoning-parser /
chat-template mapping.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------
SGLang Native APIs                        *sglang-docs-basic_usage-native_api*

Apart from the OpenAI compatible APIs, the SGLang Runtime also provides its
native server APIs. We introduce the following APIs:

- `/generate` (text generation model)
- `/get_model_info`
- `/server_info`
- `/health`
- `/health_generate`
- `/flush_cache`
- `/update_weights`
- `/encode`(embedding model)
- `/v1/rerank`(cross encoder rerank model)
- `/v1/score`(decoder-only scoring)
- `/v1/decisions`(typed decisions on a chat model)
- `/classify`(reward model)
- `/start_expert_distribution_record`
- `/stop_expert_distribution_record`
- `/dump_expert_distribution_record`
- `/tokenize`
- `/detokenize`
- A full list of these APIs can be found at http_server.py
  https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/python/sglang/srt/entrypoints/http_server.py

We mainly use `requests` to test these APIs in the following examples. You
can also use `curl`.

Admin endpoints such as `/update_weights_from_disk` and the
`/*_expert_distribution_record` APIs answer HTTP 403 unless the server is
launched with `SGLANG_ADMIN_API_KEY=<key>` set (or `--admin-api-key <key>`)
and the request carries `Authorization: Bearer <key>` (`--api-key` does not
unlock them). Once an admin key is set, `/flush_cache` requires it as well.

LAUNCH A SERVER                  *docs-basic_usage-native_api-launch-a-server*

[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    import os

    from sglang.test.doc_patch import launch_server_cmd
    from sglang.utils import wait_for_server, print_highlight, terminate_process

    os.environ["SGLANG_ADMIN_API_KEY"] = "your-admin-api-key"
    server_process, port = launch_server_cmd(
        "python3 -m sglang.launch_server --model-path qwen/qwen2.5-0.5b-instruct --host 0.0.0.0 --log-level warning"
    )

    wait_for_server(f"http://localhost:{port}", process=server_process)

    # Sent with the admin endpoints below
    admin_headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['SGLANG_ADMIN_API_KEY']}"}

GET MODEL INFO                    *docs-basic_usage-native_api-get-model-info*

Get the information of the model.

- `model_path`: The path/name of the model.
- `is_generation`: Whether the model is used as generation model or
  embedding model.
- `tokenizer_path`: The path/name of the tokenizer.
- `preferred_sampling_params`: The default sampling params specified via
  `--preferred-sampling-params`. `None` is returned in this example as we
  did not explicitly configure it in server args.
- `weight_version`: This field contains the version of the model weights.
  This is often used to track changes or updates to the model's trained
  parameters.
- `has_image_understanding`: Whether the model has image-understanding
  capability.
- `has_audio_understanding`: Whether the model has audio-understanding
  capability.
- `model_type`: The model type from the HuggingFace config (e.g., “qwen2”,
  “llama”).
- `architectures`: The model architectures from the HuggingFace config
  (e.g., [“Qwen2ForCausalLM”]).
- `embedding`: The resolved embedding-serving plan. It includes pooling,
  normalization, execution and attention style, Matryoshka dimensions, cache
  policy, and effective BCG prefill settings. This field is available when
  the model configuration exposes an embedding capability contract.

[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    url = f"http://localhost:{port}/get_model_info"

    response = requests.get(url)
    response_json = response.json()
    print_highlight(response_json)
    assert response_json["model_path"] == "qwen/qwen2.5-0.5b-instruct"
    assert response_json["is_generation"] is True
    assert response_json["tokenizer_path"] == "qwen/qwen2.5-0.5b-instruct"
    assert response_json["preferred_sampling_params"] is None
    assert response_json.keys() == {
        "model_path",
        "is_generation",
        "tokenizer_path",
        "preferred_sampling_params",
        "weight_version",
        "has_image_understanding",
        "has_audio_understanding",
        "model_type",
        "architectures",
        "embedding",
    }

HEALTH CHECK                        *docs-basic_usage-native_api-health-check*

- `/health`: Check the health of the server.
- `/health_generate`: Check the health of the server by generating one
  token.
- `/ready`: Returns 200 when the server accepts new requests; 503 while
  starting, paused, unhealthy, or shutting down.
- `/ping`: SageMaker health check. Returns 200 once the server is up; 503
  while starting, unhealthy, or shutting down. Stays 200 while generation is
  paused. A failed `/health` or `/health_generate` probe marks the server
  unhealthy until a later probe succeeds.

[Example]

    response = requests.get(url)
    print_highlight(response.text)

FLUSH CACHE                          *docs-basic_usage-native_api-flush-cache*

Flush the radix cache. It will be automatically triggered when the model
weights are updated by the `/update_weights` API.

Parameters:

- `timeout` (query, float, default `0`, unit: seconds): Wait time for idle
  state before flushing. `0` means fail fast if not idle. When HiCache async
  operations are in-flight, a non-zero timeout allows the server to wait
  until idle before flushing, avoiding unnecessary 400 errors.

[Command]

[Command]Command

>sh
    # With timeout (wait up to 30s for idle state)
    curl -s -X POST "http://127.0.0.1:30000/flush_cache?timeout=30" \
      -H "Authorization: Bearer ${SGLANG_ADMIN_API_KEY}"
<
[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    url = f"http://localhost:{port}/flush_cache"

    response = requests.post(url, headers=admin_headers)
    print_highlight(response.text)

                   *docs-basic_usage-native_api-v1/score-decoder-only-scoring*
V1/SCORE (DECODER-ONLY SCORING)

Compute token probabilities for specified tokens given a query and items.
This is useful for classification tasks, scoring responses, or computing
log-probabilities.

Parameters:

- `query`: Query text
- `items`: Item text(s) to score
- `label_token_ids`: Token IDs to compute probabilities for
- `apply_softmax`: Whether to apply softmax to get normalized probabilities
  (default: False)
- `item_first`: Whether items come first in concatenation order (default:
  False)
- `model`: Model name

`query` and `items` also accept token ids, with `query` set to `[]` when
each item is a complete prompt. `label_token_ids` can be one list per item.
`temperature` divides the label logits before the softmax and needs
`apply_softmax`, and `return_token_logprobs` adds `token_logprobs`, the
full-vocabulary log-probabilities of the labels.

The response contains `scores` - a list of probability lists, one per item,
each in the order of `label_token_ids`.

[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    score_process, port = launch_server_cmd("""
    python3 -m sglang.launch_server --model-path qwen/qwen2.5-0.5b-instruct \
        --host 0.0.0.0 --log-level warning
    """)

    wait_for_server(f"http://localhost:{port}", process=score_process)
<
[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    # Score the probability of different completions given a query
    query = "The capital of France is"
    items = ["Paris", "London", "Berlin"]

    url = f"http://localhost:{port}/v1/score"
    data = {
        "model": "qwen/qwen2.5-0.5b-instruct",
        "query": query,
        "items": items,
        "label_token_ids": [9454, 2753],  # e.g. "Yes" and "No" token ids
        "apply_softmax": True,  # Normalize probabilities to sum to 1
    }

    response = requests.post(url, json=data)
    response_json = response.json()

    # Display scores for each item
    for item, scores in zip(items, response_json["scores"]):
        print_highlight(f"Item '{item}': probabilities = {[f'{s:.4f}' for s in scores]}")
<
[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    terminate_process(score_process)
<

    *docs-basic_usage-native_api-v1/decisions-typed-decisions-on-a-chat-model*
V1/DECISIONS (TYPED DECISIONS ON A CHAT MODEL)

Answer typed questions about an input with per-option probabilities, without
generating. The server renders each question with the model's chat template
and thinking turned off, assigns one-token answer labels, and scores them
through the same path as `v1/score`.

Parameters:

- `input`: Text, object, or array the questions are about
- `questions`: List of questions, each with a unique `id` and a `type` of
  `choice` (with `options`), `score` (with `levels`), or `yes_no`
- `temperature`: Divides the label logits before the softmax (default: 1)
- `chat_template_kwargs`: Extra chat template arguments
- `prompt_format_version`: Optional pin of the server-owned prompt wording
- `return_prompt_token_ids`: Return the scored prompt and label token ids
  for replay through `v1/score` (default: False)

The response contains `answers` keyed by question id, each with `type`,
`probabilities`, and `label_mass`, plus `choice` for a choice question or
`score` for a score question. A yes or no answer is read from
`probabilities["yes"]`. See |sglang-docs-supported-models-decision_models|
for examples, the full reference, and error cases.

          *docs-basic_usage-native_api-tokenize/detokenize-example-round-trip*
TOKENIZE/DETOKENIZE EXAMPLE (ROUND TRIP)

This example demonstrates how to use the /tokenize and /detokenize endpoints
together. We first tokenize a string, then detokenize the resulting IDs to
reconstruct the original text. This workflow is useful when you need to
handle tokenization externally but still leverage the server for
detokenization.

[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    tokenizer_free_server_process, port = launch_server_cmd("""
    python3 -m sglang.launch_server --model-path qwen/qwen2.5-0.5b-instruct
    """)

    wait_for_server(f"http://localhost:{port}", process=tokenizer_free_server_process)
<
[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    import requests
    from sglang.utils import print_highlight

    base_url = f"http://localhost:{port}"
    tokenize_url = f"{base_url}/tokenize"
    detokenize_url = f"{base_url}/detokenize"

    model_name = "qwen/qwen2.5-0.5b-instruct"
    input_text = "SGLang provides efficient tokenization endpoints."
    print_highlight(f"Original Input Text:\n'{input_text}'")

    # --- tokenize the input text ---
    tokenize_payload = {
        "model": model_name,
        "prompt": input_text,
        "add_special_tokens": False,
    }
    try:
        tokenize_response = requests.post(tokenize_url, json=tokenize_payload)
        tokenize_response.raise_for_status()
        tokenization_result = tokenize_response.json()
        token_ids = tokenization_result.get("tokens")

        if not token_ids:
            raise ValueError("Tokenization returned empty tokens.")

        print_highlight(f"\nTokenized Output (IDs):\n{token_ids}")
        print_highlight(f"Token Count: {tokenization_result.get('count')}")
        print_highlight(f"Max Model Length: {tokenization_result.get('max_model_len')}")

        # --- detokenize the obtained token IDs ---
        detokenize_payload = {
            "model": model_name,
            "tokens": token_ids,
            "skip_special_tokens": True,
        }

        detokenize_response = requests.post(detokenize_url, json=detokenize_payload)
        detokenize_response.raise_for_status()
        detokenization_result = detokenize_response.json()
        reconstructed_text = detokenization_result.get("text")

        print_highlight(f"\nDetokenized Output (Text):\n'{reconstructed_text}'")

        if input_text == reconstructed_text:
            print_highlight(
                "\nRound Trip Successful: Original and reconstructed text match."
            )
        else:
            print_highlight(
                "\nRound Trip Mismatch: Original and reconstructed text differ."
            )

    except requests.exceptions.RequestException as e:
        print_highlight(f"\nHTTP Request Error: {e}")
    except Exception as e:
        print_highlight(f"\nAn error occurred: {e}")
<
[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    terminate_process(tokenizer_free_server_process)
<
`/tokenize` also accepts chat `messages` (with optional `tools` and
`chat_template_kwargs`) in place of `prompt`. By default they are rendered
as for a chat completion: a final assistant message becomes a user turn and
the generation prompt is always added. To format messages exactly as given,
pass `add_generation_prompt` (`true` or `false`); the request may then also
set `add_special_tokens`, which defaults to `false` because the chat
template writes its own special tokens. These options need a Jinja chat
template; other templates return HTTP 400.

    prompts = [
        "Write a short, neutral self-introduction for a fictional character. Hello, my name is",

       *docs-basic_usage-offline_engine_api-streaming-asynchronous-generation*
Streaming Asynchronous Generation

[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    prompts = [
        "Write a short, neutral self-introduction for a fictional character. Hello, my name is",
        "Provide a concise factual statement about France’s capital city. The capital of France is",
        "Explain possible future trends in artificial intelligence. The future of AI is",
    ]

    sampling_params = {"temperature": 0.8, "top_p": 0.95}

    print("\n=== Testing asynchronous streaming generation (no repeats) ===")

    async def main():
        for prompt in prompts:
            print(f"\nPrompt: {prompt}")
            print("Generated text: ", end="", flush=True)

            # Replace direct calls to async_generate with our custom overlap-aware version
            async for cleaned_chunk in async_stream_and_merge(llm, prompt, sampling_params):
                print(cleaned_chunk, end="", flush=True)

            print()  # New line after each prompt

    asyncio.run(main())

    *docs-basic_usage-openai_api_completions-model-thinking/reasoning-support*
Model Thinking/Reasoning Support

Some models support internal reasoning or thinking processes that can be
exposed in the API response. SGLang provides unified support for various
reasoning models through the `chat_template_kwargs` parameter and compatible
reasoning parsers.

  *docs-basic_usage-openai_api_completions-supported-models-and-configuration*
Supported Models and Configuration

Model Family      Chat Template     Reasoning Parser    Notes
                  Parameter
----------------  ----------------  ------------------  ----------------------
DeepSeek-R1 (R1,  enable_thinking   --reasoning-parser  Standard reasoning
R1-0528,                            deepseek-r1         models
R1-Distill)
DeepSeek-V3.1     thinking          --reasoning-parser  Hybrid model
                                    deepseek-v3         (thinking/non-thinking
                                                        modes)
Qwen3 (standard)  enable_thinking   --reasoning-parser  Hybrid model
                                    qwen3               (thinking/non-thinking
                                                        modes)
Qwen3-Thinking    N/A (always       --reasoning-parser  Always generates
                  enabled)          qwen3-thinking      reasoning
Kimi              N/A (always       --reasoning-parser  Kimi thinking models
                  enabled)          kimi
Gpt-Oss           N/A (always       --reasoning-parser  Gpt-Oss thinking
                  enabled)          gpt-oss             models

Basic Usage              *docs-basic_usage-openai_api_completions-basic-usage*

To use reasoning output:

1. Launch the server with the appropriate reasoning parser.
2. Use the model-specific parameter in `chat_template_kwargs` when you need
   to override the model's chat-template default.
3. Optionally use `separate_reasoning: False` to keep reasoning in the
   response content instead of returning it separately (defaults to `True`).

  Note: ~

  Note for Qwen3-Thinking models: These models always generate thinking
  content and do not support the `enable_thinking` parameter. Use
  `--reasoning-parser qwen3-thinking` or `--reasoning-parser qwen3` to parse
  the thinking content.

                *docs-basic_usage-openai_api_completions-example-qwen3-models*
Example: Qwen3 Models

[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    # Launch server:
    # python3 -m sglang.launch_server --model Qwen/Qwen3-4B --reasoning-parser qwen3

    from openai import OpenAI

    client = OpenAI(
        api_key="EMPTY",
        base_url=f"http://127.0.0.1:30000/v1",
    )

    model = "Qwen/Qwen3-4B"
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "How many r's are in 'strawberry'?"}]

    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model=model,
        messages=messages,
        extra_body={
            "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": True},
            "separate_reasoning": True
        }
    )

    print("Reasoning:", response.choices[0].message.reasoning_content)
    print("-"*100)
    print("Answer:", response.choices[0].message.content)
<
ExampleOutput:

[Output]

[Output]Output

>text
    Reasoning: Okay, so the user is asking how many 'r's are in the word 'strawberry'. Let me think. First, I need to make sure I have the word spelled correctly. Strawberry... S-T-R-A-W-B-E-R-R-Y. Wait, is that right? Let me break it down.

    Starting with 'strawberry', let's write out the letters one by one. S, T, R, A, W, B, E, R, R, Y. Hmm, wait, that's 10 letters. Let me check again. S (1), T (2), R (3), A (4), W (5), B (6), E (7), R (8), R (9), Y (10). So the letters are S-T-R-A-W-B-E-R-R-Y.
    ...
    Therefore, the answer should be three R's in 'strawberry'. But I need to make sure I'm not counting any other letters as R. Let me check again. S, T, R, A, W, B, E, R, R, Y. No other R's. So three in total. Yeah, that seems right.

    ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    Answer: The word "strawberry" contains **three** letters 'r'. Here's the breakdown:

    1. **S-T-R-A-W-B-E-R-R-Y**
       - The **third letter** is 'R'.
       - The **eighth and ninth letters** are also 'R's.

    Thus, the total count is **3**.

    **Answer:** 3.
<
  Note: ~

  Setting `"enable_thinking": False` disables reasoning for Qwen3. Omitting
  the parameter follows the model's chat-template default; Qwen3 enables
  thinking by default. Qwen3-Thinking models always generate reasoning
  content and do not support the `enable_thinking` parameter.

*docs-basic_usage-openai_api_completions-set-a-default-for-openai-chat-completions*
Set a Default for OpenAI Chat Completions

If most OpenAI chat-completion requests should use the same chat-template
mode, set a default when launching the server:

[Command]

[Command]Command

>sh
    python -m sglang.launch_server \
      --model-path Qwen/Qwen3-4B \
      --reasoning-parser qwen3 \
      --default-chat-template-kwargs '{"enable_thinking": false}'
<
`--default-chat-template-kwargs` accepts a JSON object and merges it into
each OpenAI chat-completion request's `chat_template_kwargs`. For ordinary
template keys such as `enable_thinking`, the precedence is:

1. An explicit value in the request's `chat_template_kwargs`
2. The value in `--default-chat-template-kwargs`
3. The model's chat-template default

`reasoning_effort` follows a separate normalization path, so the precedence
list above does not apply to it. Configure `reasoning_effort` in either the
server defaults or individual requests, not both.

The accepted keys are model-specific. For example, Qwen3 uses
`enable_thinking`, while other model families may use `thinking` or may not
expose a reasoning toggle. The reasoning parser controls how reasoning
tokens are separated from the response; it does not by itself enable
reasoning in the chat template.

                  *docs-basic_usage-openai_api_completions-logit-bias-support*
Logit Bias Support

SGLang supports the `logit_bias` parameter for both chat completions and
completions APIs. This parameter allows you to modify the likelihood of
specific tokens being generated by adding bias values to their logits. As in
the OpenAI API, bias values are normally in the range -100 to 100, where:

- Positive values (0 to 100) increase the likelihood of the token being
  selected
- Negative values (-100 to 0) decrease the likelihood of the token being
  selected
- -100 effectively prevents the token from being generated

The `logit_bias` parameter accepts a dictionary where keys are token IDs (as
strings) and values are the bias amounts (as floats).

SGLang does not restrict values to -100 to 100; it only requires them to be
finite with a magnitude of at most `1e30` (see
|docs-basic_usage-openai_api_completions-parameter-validation|).

Getting Token IDs  *docs-basic_usage-openai_api_completions-getting-token-ids*

To use `logit_bias` effectively, you need to know the token IDs for the
words you want to bias. Here's how to get token IDs:

[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    # Get tokenizer to find token IDs
    import tiktoken

    # For OpenAI models, use the appropriate encoding
    tokenizer = tiktoken.encoding_for_model("gpt-3.5-turbo")  # or your model

    # Get token IDs for specific words
    word = "sunny"
    token_ids = tokenizer.encode(word)
    print(f"Token IDs for '{word}': {token_ids}")

    # For SGLang models, you can access the tokenizer through the client
    # and get token IDs for bias
<
  Tip: ~

  Important: The `logit_bias` parameter uses token IDs as string keys, not
  the actual words.

          *docs-basic_usage-openai_api_completions-example-deepseek-v3-models*

    I need to count the number of times the letter 'r' appears in the word "strawberry".

    Let me write out the word: S-T-R-A-W-B-E-R-R-Y.

    Now, I'll go through each letter and count the 'r's.
    ...

[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    # Example with logit_bias parameter
    # Note: You need to get the actual token IDs from your tokenizer
    # For demonstration, we'll use some example token IDs
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="qwen/qwen2.5-0.5b-instruct",
        messages=[
            {"role": "user", "content": "Complete this sentence: The weather today is"}

        max_tokens=20,

            "12345": 50,  # Increase likelihood of token ID 12345
            "67890": -50,  # Decrease likelihood of token ID 67890
            "11111": 25,  # Slightly increase likelihood of token ID 11111
        },

Parameters                *docs-basic_usage-openai_api_completions-parameters*

The chat completions API accepts OpenAI Chat Completions API's parameters.
Refer to OpenAI Chat Completions API
https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/chat/create for more details.

SGLang extends the standard API with the `extra_body` parameter, allowing
for additional customization. One key option within `extra_body` is
`chat_template_kwargs`, which can be used to pass arguments to the chat
template processor.

[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="qwen/qwen2.5-0.5b-instruct",
        messages=[
            {
                "role": "system",
                "content": "You are a knowledgeable historian who provides concise responses.",
            },
            {"role": "user", "content": "Tell me about ancient Rome"},
            {
                "role": "assistant",
                "content": "Ancient Rome was a civilization centered in Italy.",
            },
            {"role": "user", "content": "What were their major achievements?"},
        ],
        temperature=0.3,  # Lower temperature for more focused responses
        max_tokens=128,  # Reasonable length for a concise response
        top_p=0.95,  # Slightly higher for better fluency
        presence_penalty=0.2,  # Mild penalty to avoid repetition
        frequency_penalty=0.2,  # Mild penalty for more natural language
        n=1,  # Single response is usually more stable
        seed=42,  # Keep for reproducibility
    )

    print_highlight(response.choices[0].message.content)
<
Streaming mode is also supported.

                *docs-basic_usage-openai_api_completions-parameter-validation*
Parameter Validation

Requests with invalid sampling parameters are rejected with HTTP 400 before
generation starts. This also applies when `stream=true`: the first chunk is
read before the stream is opened, so the error is returned as a regular HTTP
400 response and not as part of an event stream.

Parameter                 Accepted values            Applies to
------------------------  -------------------------  -------------------------
n                         Integer from 1 to 128      Chat completions and
                                                     completions
max_tokens,               Integer greater than or    Chat completions
max_completion_tokens     equal to 0; booleans are
                          rejected
temperature               Finite number greater      Chat completions
                          than or equal to 0
                          (negative, inf and nan
                          are rejected)
top_logprobs              Integer greater than or    Chat completions
                          equal to 0; with
                          logprobs=true it must
                          also not exceed the
                          vocabulary size
logit_bias values         Finite numbers with a      Chat completions and
                          magnitude of at most 1e30  completions

For chat completions, `max_completion_tokens` takes precedence over
`max_tokens` when both are set, including an explicit
`max_completion_tokens=0`, which generates no tokens and returns
`finish_reason="length"`. The completions API still requires `max_tokens` to
be greater than 0.

SGLang deliberately does not enforce the following OpenAI limits and applies
the given values as they are: `temperature` of at most 2, `top_logprobs` of
at most 20, `logit_bias` values within -100 to 100, and `logprobs=true`
being required for `top_logprobs`.

                *docs-basic_usage-openai_api_completions-logit-bias-support-2*
Logit Bias Support

The completions API also supports the `logit_bias` parameter with the same
functionality as described in the chat completions section above.

[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    stream = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="qwen/qwen2.5-0.5b-instruct",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Say this is a test"}],
        stream=True,
    )
    for chunk in stream:
        if chunk.choices[0].delta.content is not None:
            print(chunk.choices[0].delta.content, end="")
<

 *docs-basic_usage-openai_api_completions-returning-routed-experts-moe-models*
Returning Routed Experts (MoE Models)

For MoE models, set `return_routed_experts: true` in `extra_body` to return
expert routing data. Requires `--enable-return-routed-experts` server flag.
By default, `routed_experts` is returned in the response-level `sglext`
object as base64-encoded int32 expert IDs in a flattened array with logical
shape `[num_tokens, num_layers, top_k]`. For non-streaming chat responses
with `return_meta_info: true`, `routed_experts` is returned only in each
choice's `meta_info` object and omitted from response-level `sglext` to
avoid duplicating the routing data. Other requested extension fields, such
as `cached_tokens_details` and `spec_tokens_details`, remain in
response-level `sglext`. By default, routed experts cover `[0, seqlen - 1)`,
the full available sequence, because RL workflows need them for the full
sequence. Set `routed_experts_start_len` in `extra_body` to an absolute
prefix length to return only `[routed_experts_start_len, seqlen - 1)`. For
example, in multi-turn RL rollouts, routed experts for tokens from previous
turns have already been collected, so setting this value avoids unnecessary
transfer that causes bottlenecks.

  *docs-basic_usage-openai_api_completions-returning-flat-output-top-logprobs*
Returning Flat Output Top Logprobs

With `logprobs: true` and `top_logprobs: k`, set
`return_flat_raw_output_top_logprobs: true` and `return_meta_info: true` in
`extra_body` to receive the output top logprobs as flat arrays in each
choice's `meta_info` instead of nested objects. This skips detokenizing
every candidate and shrinks the response, which matters for large `k`. The
arrays arrive with the finished response only, so `stream: true` is not
supported. `choices[].logprobs` still carries the selected-token logprobs,
but its `top_logprobs` lists are empty.

`meta_info` then carries `output_top_logprobs_shape` (`[rows, k]`) and
`output_top_logprobs_null_prefix`; covered position `i`, rank `j` sits at
flat index `(i - null_prefix) * k + j`. On chat completions the arrays are
base64 by default: `output_top_logprobs_{val,idx}_flat_b64`, little-endian
bytes whose dtypes are given by the `_dtype` fields (float32 and int32), so
non-finite logprobs such as `-inf` survive. Set
`return_flat_raw_top_logprobs_b64: false` for plain JSON lists in
`output_top_logprobs_{val,idx}_flat`. The native `/generate` API takes the
same fields, with base64 off by default.

>python
    import base64

    import numpy as np

    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="qwen/qwen2.5-0.5b-instruct",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Say this is a test"}],
        max_tokens=16,
        logprobs=True,
        top_logprobs=5,
        extra_body={"return_meta_info": True, "return_flat_raw_output_top_logprobs": True},
    )
    meta = response.choices[0].meta_info
    shape = meta["output_top_logprobs_shape"]
    val = np.frombuffer(
        base64.b64decode(meta["output_top_logprobs_val_flat_b64"]),
        dtype=meta["output_top_logprobs_val_flat_b64_dtype"],
    ).reshape(shape)
    idx = np.frombuffer(
        base64.b64decode(meta["output_top_logprobs_idx_flat_b64"]),
        dtype=meta["output_top_logprobs_idx_flat_b64_dtype"],
    ).reshape(shape)
<

       *docs-basic_usage-openai_api_completions-returning-flat-sampling-masks*
Returning Flat Sampling Masks

With `return_sampling_mask: true`, set `return_flat_raw_sampling_mask: true`
and `return_meta_info: true` in `extra_body` to receive the sampling masks
as flat arrays in each choice's `meta_info` instead of one nested list per
output token. The arrays arrive with the finished response only, so
`stream: true` is not supported.

`meta_info` then carries `output_token_sampling_mask_flat` (every row's
token ids, row after row), `output_token_sampling_mask_row_lengths` (one row
length per output token) and `output_token_sampling_logprobs_flat` (one
logprob per token id in `support` mode, one per row in `selected` mode). On
chat completions they are base64 by default, under `_b64` keys whose dtypes
are given by the `_dtype` fields (int32, int32 and float32). Set
`return_flat_raw_sampling_mask_b64: false` for plain JSON lists. The native
`/generate` API takes the same fields, with base64 off by default.

>python
    meta = response.choices[0].meta_info
    lengths = np.frombuffer(
        base64.b64decode(meta["output_token_sampling_mask_row_lengths_b64"]),
        dtype=meta["output_token_sampling_mask_row_lengths_b64_dtype"],
    )
    token_ids = np.frombuffer(
        base64.b64decode(meta["output_token_sampling_mask_flat_b64"]),
        dtype=meta["output_token_sampling_mask_flat_b64_dtype"],
    )
    rows = np.split(token_ids, np.cumsum(lengths)[:-1])
<
[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    # Example with logit_bias parameter for completions API
    # Note: You need to get the actual token IDs from your tokenizer
    # For demonstration, we'll use some example token IDs
    response = client.completions.create(
        model="qwen/qwen2.5-0.5b-instruct",
        prompt="The best programming language for AI is",
        temperature=0.7,
        max_tokens=20,
        logit_bias={
            "12345": 75,  # Strongly favor token ID 12345
            "67890": -100,  # Completely avoid token ID 67890
            "11111": -25,  # Slightly discourage token ID 11111
        },
    )

    print_highlight(f"Response with logit bias: {response.choices[0].text}")
<

COMPLETIONS              *docs-basic_usage-openai_api_completions-completions*

        max_tokens=64,
        n=1,
        stop=None,

Parameters              *docs-basic_usage-openai_api_completions-parameters-2*

The completions API accepts OpenAI Completions API's parameters. Refer to
OpenAI Completions API
https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/completions/create for more
details.

Here is an example of a detailed completions request:

[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    response = client.completions.create(
        model="qwen/qwen2.5-0.5b-instruct",
        prompt="Write a short story about a space explorer.",
        temperature=0.7,  # Moderate temperature for creative writing
        max_tokens=150,  # Longer response for a story
        top_p=0.9,  # Balanced diversity in word choice
        stop=["\n\n", "THE END"],  # Multiple stop sequences
        presence_penalty=0.3,  # Encourage novel elements
        frequency_penalty=0.3,  # Reduce repetitive phrases
        n=1,  # Generate one completion
        seed=123,  # For reproducible results
    )

    print_highlight(f"Response: {response}")
<

*docs-basic_usage-openai_api_completions-returning-routed-experts-moe-models-2*
Returning Routed Experts (MoE Models)

For MoE models, set `return_routed_experts: true` in `extra_body` to return
expert routing data. Requires `--enable-return-routed-experts` server flag.
The `routed_experts` field will be returned in the `sgl_ext` object on each
choice, containing base64-encoded int32 expert IDs as a flattened array with
logical shape `[num_tokens, num_layers, top_k]`. By default this returns
`[0, seqlen - 1)`, the full available sequence, because RL workflows need
routed experts for the full sequence. Set `routed_experts_start_len` in
`extra_body` to an absolute prefix length to return only
`[routed_experts_start_len, seqlen - 1)`. For example, in multi-turn RL
rollouts, routed experts for tokens from previous turns have already been
collected, so setting this value avoids unnecessary transfer that cause
bottlenecks.

                 *docs-basic_usage-openai_api_completions-using-lora-adapters*
USING LORA ADAPTERS

SGLang supports LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) adapters with OpenAI-compatible
APIs. You can specify which adapter to use directly in the `model` parameter
using the `base-model:adapter-name` syntax.

Server Setup:

[Command]

[Command]Command

>sh
    python -m sglang.launch_server \
        --model-path qwen/qwen2.5-0.5b-instruct \
        --enable-lora \
        --lora-paths adapter_a=/path/to/adapter_a adapter_b=/path/to/adapter_b
<
For more details on LoRA serving configuration, see the
|sglang-docs-advanced_features-lora|.

API Call:

(Recommended) Use the `model:adapter` syntax to specify which adapter to
use:

[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="qwen/qwen2.5-0.5b-instruct:adapter_a",  # ← base-model:adapter-name
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Convert to SQL: show all users"}],
        max_tokens=50,
    )
<
Backward Compatible: Using `extra_body`

The old `extra_body` method is still supported for backward compatibility:

[Example]

[Example]Example

>python
    # Backward compatible method
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="qwen/qwen2.5-0.5b-instruct",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Convert to SQL: show all users"}],
        extra_body={"lora_path": "adapter_a"},  # ← old method
        max_tokens=50,
    )
<
Note: When both `model:adapter` and `extra_body["lora_path"]` are specified,
the `model:adapter` syntax takes precedence.

[Example]Example

>python
    terminate_process(server_process)
